THEOBROMA: an aggregated open database of 1.13 million natural products with per-compound license auditing, three-tier classification, and stereochemistry-aware deduplication
works.abstract: Abstract Natural products remain one of the most productive sources of pharmacologically active compounds for drug discovery. Open aggregators attribute licenses at database granularity, and the consequences of that choice have become tangible as the field grows. A recent relicensing event in one constituent source (the September 2024 transition of the Natural Products Atlas to CC BY-NC 4.0) demonstrates how database-level licensing propagates across an aggregate and motivates the per-compound audit framework presented here. The same peer cohort separately leaves classification provenance and stereoisomer-family relations coarser than either layer warrants. THEOBROMA, accessible at https://theobroma.l3s.uni-hannover.de, integrates 1 132 805 natural products from 29 open sources under a per-compound license audit that resolves each compound’s license tier across all attesting sources under a most-restrictive-wins rule. 896 242 compounds (79.12%) are identified under open-use licenses, and the per-source attestation chain, together with the resolved tier, is exposed through a dedicated audit endpoint and a query-time license filter. A three-tier classification labels all but 21 compounds by the provenance of the assignment (55.3% curated source labels, 18.2% NPClassifier tool assignments, 26.5% model-inferred). Deduplication at the full 27-character InChIKey retains 1 132 805 entries across 486 032 connectivity families, exposed via a dedicated /api/stereoisomers/<comp_id> endpoint and a radial-family display. Any result set renders directly onto a taxonomic cladogram of its source organisms, so compositional queries are answered in the interface rather than downstream. Per-compound license provenance is the primary differentiator, while classification stratification and stereoisomer-family exposure add finer-grained access to two related axes. Together, they support license-compatible virtual screening and isomer-specific bioactivity analysis at corpus scale. As an evolving open resource, THEOBROMA pairs continuous pipeline maintenance with interactive geographic, taxonomic, and chemical-space exploration.

works.title: RNAactDrug 2.0: an updated resource for systematically exploring molecular features associated with drug sensitivity across multi-omics datasets
works.abstract: RNAactDrug 2.0 (available at https://bio-bigdata.hrbmu.edu.cn/RNAactDrug or https://bio-datamining.hrbmu.edu.cn/RNAactDrug) is an updated resource for systematically exploring molecular features associated with drug sensitivity across multi-omics datasets. We have updated the RNAactDrug 2.0 database with significantly expanded data and improved features, including (i) ∼30 000 drugs, 38 908 RNA molecules, and 22 800 375 drug-RNA associations from large-scale pharmacogenomic databases, covering four molecular layers: expression, copy number variation (CNV), mutation, and methylation; (ii) 11 099 cases from The Cancer Genome Atlas across 33 cancer types are integrated to support clinical and pan-cancer analyses of drug sensitivity-associated RNA features; (iii) ∼3.8 million cells from >200 single-cell RNA sequencing datasets, spanning 34 cancer types and 38 tissues, enable analysis of cell type-specific patterns and intratumoral heterogeneity; (iv) 26 440 enhancers and 788 444 drug-enhancer associations, combined with potential target prediction, provide an exploratory epigenetic regulatory dimension; (v) enhanced search and browsing functionalities, together with seven tools for functional annotation, pan-cancer analysis, tumor microenvironment profiling, single-cell trajectory and CNV analysis, and enhancer-related analyses. In summary, RNAactDrug 2.0 is a crucial resource for the multi-omics dissection of drug sensitivity-associated molecules, providing important support for the discovery of drug resistance biomarkers and the advancement of personalized therapeutic strategies.

works.title: InterPro: the protein sequence classification resource in 2027
works.abstract: InterPro (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/interpro) is a freely accessible resource for the classification of protein sequences. It integrates predictive models, known as signatures, from multiple member databases to classify sequences into families and to predict the presence of domains and functionally important sites. The InterPro database provides annotations for hundreds of millions of sequences, ensuring extensive coverage of UniProtKB, the standard repository of protein sequences, and includes mapping to several other major resources, such as Gene Ontology, the Protein Data Bank in Europe (PDBe), and the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database. In this publication we report on the status of InterPro (version 110.0), detailing new developments in the database, its associated web interface, and software. Notable updates include InterPro-N, a deep-learning method that increases sequence coverage of UniProtKB to over 90%; the transition from InterProScan 5 to the completely re-engineered InterProScan 6; the integration of structure-based domain classifications and predicted structures from AlphaFold; a redesigned protein viewer offering a concise summary view; and a new Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that allows AI assistants to query InterPro programmatically. Over the past two years, 9484 new InterPro entries have been created, bringing the total to 54 922. InterPro data, software and tools are freely available.

works.title: The TCR Motif Atlas: a database of specificities for TCRs recognizing viral, cancer, and autoimmune epitopes
works.abstract: T-cell recognition is elicited by the binding between T-cell receptors (TCRs) and epitopes. Many machine learning approaches have been proposed to model TCR-epitope recognition specificity, but most of them act as black boxes. To visualize TCR-epitope recognition specificity, we developed the TCR Motif Atlas (https://tcrmotifatlas.unil.ch). This database builds upon the probabilistic framework of TCR specificity profiles (TSPs) to visualize V and J genes as well as complementarity-determining Region 3 (CDR3) lengths and amino acids enriched in epitope-specific TCRs with respect to baseline TCR repertoires for hundreds of epitopes. An interactive interface enables users to build TSPs based on their own set of TCR sequences to investigate epitope recognition specificity or to explore potential biases in TCR repertoires of known or undetermined specificity. The TCR Motif Atlas further provides links to curated compilations of epitope-specific TCRs and crystal structures of TCR-epitope complexes.

works.title: CircaVal: a gene-centric multi-omics platform for exploring circadian regulatory features
works.abstract: The circadian clock orchestrates daily physiological processes through coordinated regulation of clock-controlled gene expression across multiple molecular layers. However, systematic characterization of this multilayered rhythmic regulation remains challenging because relevant information is distributed across independent datasets and rhythmicity is evaluated using diverse analytical approaches. Here, we developed CircaVal, a gene-centric multi-omics platform for the integrated exploration and interpretation of circadian regulatory features in humans, mice, and baboons. To support this framework, CircaVal processes public datasets using standardized, data-type-specific pipelines, and gene rhythmicity is integrated with tissue-specific expression, cross-species orthology, functional annotations, and multi-omics regulatory features. CircaVal further introduces an integrated rhythmicity score (IRS), which combines concordance across multiple rhythm-detection methods with reproducibility across independent datasets to provide a quantitative basis for prioritizing candidate rhythmic genes. The platform enables users to examine gene rhythmicity across datasets, identify tissue-enriched rhythmic genes, compare rhythmicity across species, and explore associated regulatory features. Additional functions include interactive gene-centric exploration, genome-browser visualization, rhythmicity analysis of user-uploaded time-series data, and programmatic data access. Together, these capabilities provide an integrated framework for rhythmic gene prioritization and gene-level interpretation of circadian regulatory features across tissues, species, datasets, and omics data types. CircaVal is freely available at https://CircaVal.com.

works.title: tModBase v2.0: an expanded database of tRNA modifications with an AI-powered assistant
works.abstract: Chemical modifications of transfer RNAs (tRNAs) are crucial for tRNA stability, codon decoding, translational fidelity, and tRNA-derived small RNA (tsRNA) biogenesis. Changes in these modifications are associated with stress responses, physiological regulation, and human disease, underscoring the need to integrate modification information with experimental evidence and biological context. We previously established tModBase, a web resource to organize and explore tRNA modification-related data. Its first release integrated modification sites, high-throughput sequencing-derived signals, and condition-dependent changes. Since then, tRNA profiling has expanded through modification-specific and direct RNA sequencing strategies, with rapidly growing datasets across species and conditions. Here, we present tModBase v2.0 (http://www.tmodbase2.com/), containing 528 datasets across 23 species, 40 sequencing and library-preparation methods, and 42 modification types. It includes 68 third-generation and 210 modification-specific sequencing datasets, extending coverage of direct-RNA and modification-specific approaches. tModBase v2.0 further integrates sequencing-derived signals, condition-dependent information, and biological annotations linking modifications with enzymes, genetic variants, tsRNAs, diseases, and expression profiles. The LLM- and retrieval-augmented generation-powered assistant tModBot enables natural-language exploration across database modules while grounding responses in retrieved tModBase evidence. tModBase v2.0 therefore provides an expanded resource for investigating the diversity, dynamics, and biological context of tRNA modifications.

works.title: The European Nucleotide Archive in 2026
works.abstract: The European Nucleotide Archive (ENA, https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena), hosted at EMBL's European Bioinformatics Institute, is an open resource that supports the global life sciences community by enabling submission, archiving, dissemination, and reuse of the world's nucleotide sequencing data. In 2026, the ENA continues to explore and address challenges related to a rapidly evolving landscape. This includes sustaining the growth of the data volume, increasing diversity in data types, the need for more standardized metadata, and the connection of sequence data with data from other disciplines. To address these challenges, the ENA has enhanced its services to adopt the INSDC minimum specification for data requirements, introduce new sample checklists and collaborate on an experiment checklist, and progress on the implementation of GFF3 for annotations. The ENA continues to support global science through its global engagement that includes understanding its Access and Benefit Sharing (ABS) requirements to the wider community. Sustainability is a major aspect of the archive, which has seen updates to incremental indexing and SRA read removal. Additionally, the broker community continues to be supported and expanded. In this paper, we discuss these challenges and opportunities as we continue to keep pace with the evolving life science data resource ecosystem and requirements.

works.title: CDC7 and CDK8 kinases cooperate to support DNA replication origin firing in human cells
works.abstract: The coordinated activation of DNA replication origins is important for efficient DNA synthesis and genome stability. S-phase cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs), together with CDC7 kinase, are essential for origin activation by converting the pre-replicative complex into a fully active helicase. Here, in order to identify genes that tune DNA replication, we performed a chemogenetic genome-wide CRISPR-KO screen in cells challenged with the CDC7 inhibitor XL413. By developing a methodology based on genetic co-essentiality to functionally cluster the hits, we uncover the transcriptional CDK8/CCNC kinase in a cluster with replication initiation factors. Depletion of CDK8 further reduces the rate of DNA synthesis imposed by CDC7 inhibitors. DNA fibre experiments further support that CDK8 and CDC7 cooperate in origin activation. Suppression of DNA synthesis by CDK8 inhibition requires the binding of CDK8/CCNC to the MDM2 Binding Protein (MTBP), and we show that CDC7 and CDK8 associate with the MCM complex and individually contribute to the phosphorylation of the replicative helicase. In conclusion, this work adds CDK8 to the list of kinases directly involved in origin activation in human cells.

works.title: Comprehensive proteomic profiling reveals mRNA splicing suppression during human oocyte aging
works.abstract: Reproductive aging impairs female fertility, and oocyte aging is considered a major driver of this phenotype, which manifests with increased aneuploidy and miscarriage risk, while no effective treatments have been widely implemented to date. Here, we report comprehensive protein expression profiling of oocytes during human aging, comparing fully grown germinal vesicle oocytes (FGO) and metaphase II (MII) oocytes; we describe the effect of aging on the maturation profiles across multiple age groups, including 25, 30, 35, and 40 years old. This analysis uncovered differential protein dynamics upon aging, with FGOs displaying protein expression alterations as early as 30 years, whereas these changes were delayed until the age of 35 or 40 in MII oocytes, particularly in proteins associated with mRNA splicing, translation, and chromosome segregation. Integration with transcriptomic data revealed suppression of splicing machineries as a potential initiating factor driving oocyte aging, characterized by deficiencies in mitochondrial function and chromosome segregation. This was validated by splicing inhibition, which suppressed mitochondrial function and ROS levels in mouse and human oocytes. Further, splicing factor DHX15 was identified as a candidate regulator of stage-specific oocyte aging. Together, our work systematically delineates the dynamic protein landscapes of human oocytes across multiple age groups, providing molecular targets and potential therapeutic strategies for clinical intervention.

works.title: Safe lysosomal sequestration of ferrous iron is mediated via cholesterol shielding and drives senescence and ferroptosis resistance
works.abstract: Abstract Iron accumulation is a conserved hallmark of cellular as well as organismal aging, yet its mechanistic role in senescence remains largely elusive. Here we show that the accumulation of ferrous iron (Fe 2+ ) in lysosomes, a unique feature of senescent cells, is crucial for the induction of multiple senescence-associated phenotypes. Intriguingly, we found that this lysosomal Fe 2+ sequestration is rendered “safe” by a dual metabolic adaptation that confers robust resistance to ferroptosis. First, Fe 2+ accumulation triggers lysosomal alkalinization and subsequent cholesterol accumulation, which reinforces the lysosomal membrane against permeabilization. Second, senescent cells partition polyunsaturated fatty acids into lipid droplets, thereby depleting these ferroptosis-prone substrates from cellular membranes. Our findings establish that such cholesterol-enabled safe sequestration of Fe 2+ serves as a central modulator linking senescence-associated remodeling to ferroptosis resistance. Modulating this lysosomal iron-centered pathway may provide new opportunities to target and control the behavior of senescent cells.

works.title: Adjusting for medication status in genome-wide association studies
works.abstract: When conducting genome-wide association studies, addressing medication status that is relevant to the trait of interest can prevent biases that could distort estimates of the true genetic effect. Here, we introduce the genetic empirical medication reduction adjustment (GEMRA) method which uses a heuristic search for an empirical adjustment to be applied to phenotypic values of participants reporting medication use. Through simulations we show that the direct genetic effect estimates in the GEMRA approach exhibited less bias and greater statistical power than common strategies such as including medication as a covariate, restricting the sample to unmedicated users or including all samples without adjustment. We then applied the GEMRA approach to estimate statin medication adjustment for analysis of low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol levels and antihypertensive medication adjustment for analyses of systolic (SBP) and diastolic (DBP) blood pressure using multi-population data from UK Biobank and the Uganda Genome Resource. We found that a relative rather than an absolute adjustment better modelled the effect of medication on LDL cholesterol, SBP and DBP, with an effect of 40%, 10% and 10% reduction appearing to be consistent across populations, respectively. We also show that spurious differences in medication effects across populations can arise when the effect scale is misspecified.

works.title: A common pathogenic founder variant in Rwandan breast cancer cases
works.abstract: Germline data from African populations remain sparse, limiting characterization of population-specific BRCA1/2 pathogenic variants (PV). In a study of 175 Rwandan women with breast cancer, 7 unrelated carriers (4% of cases; 22% of PV carriers) harbored the same BRCA1 frameshift PVs, c.4065_4068del (p.Asn1355Lysfs*10), which is extremely rare in gnomAD yet recurrent in European, Asian, and Middle Eastern cohorts. Whole-exome sequencing and haplotype analysis of all 7 carriers revealed a shared ancestral block of approximately 581 kb surrounding the variant, and extended haplotype homozygosity and network analyses confirmed a common founder origin. Coalescent-based age estimation placed the founder event approximately 4,000--10,000 years ago. Comparison with 1000 Genomes Project data showed the founder haplotype is absent or exceedingly rare outside African and South Asian populations. These findings strongly suggest the c.4065_4068del variant as a pre-historical BRCA1 founder variant in Rwanda, with implications for targeted genetic testing, cascade screening, and cancer prevention in the region.

works.title: Genetic architecture of the murine serum metabolome reveals carboxyl esterases as master regulators of circulating fatty acid metabolism
works.abstract: BACKGROUND: The systemic biochemical diversity of circulating metabolites and lipids reflects the integrated effects of genetic variation and environmental exposure. Metabolite quantitative trait locus (mQTL) studies in humans have established gene-metabolite associations, but genetic contributions can be obscured by sex, diet, age, medication use, and environmental exposures. Genetically diverse model systems offer a powerful complementary strategy to isolate genetic contributions to the biochemical diversity of the circulating metabolome. METHODOLOGY/PRINCIPAL FINDINGS: We applied mass spectrometry profiling to serum samples in 541 mice from the Diversity Outbred (DO) population and identified 1,933 mQTL across 240 metabolites, 561 lipids, 43 oxylipins, and 4,465 MS/MS features. QTL hotspots on chromosomes 8, 9, 10, and 17 implicated distinct loci in the regulation of serum lipids, metabolites, and peptide-like features. The chromosome 8 Ces1 and Ces2 gene clusters were associated with lipids, acylcarnitines, and acyl-CoAs, while chromosomes 9 and 10 loci included additional lipid and metabolite QTL. On chromosome 17, MHC and C3 regions were associated with untargeted peptide-like MS/MS features. Comparisons with matched red blood cell mQTL revealed widespread compartment-specific genetic control. CONCLUSIONS/SIGNIFICANCE: Collectively, these findings provide a high-resolution map of the genetic regulation of the circulating metabolome, offering mechanistic insights that complement and extend human metabolic genetics.

works.title: Enhancing cell type deconvolution in spatial transcriptomics through incorporating multiple reference panels
works.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) captures gene expression with spatial context but often at resolutions where each spatial location contains multiple cells. Deconvolution of cell-type proportions is therefore essential, yet existing methods typically rely on a single scRNA-seq reference, limiting accuracy when references are incomplete or mismatched especially in complex tissues. These limitations highlight the need for a framework that can integrate multiple references while leveraging spatial information. We introduce SWIMR (Spatially Weighted Integration for Multi-Reference deconvolution), a statistical framework that integrates multiple scRNA-seq references while accounting for spatial correlations. SWIMR models each spatial location as a weighted combination of references, with both cell-type proportions and reference weights varying across tissue locations. Across comprehensive simulations and diverse ST datasets, SWIMR consistently outperformed single-reference approaches. In developing human heart tissue, it recovered ground-truth cell-type compositions with the highest accuracy. In human lung and breast cancer, SWIMR delineated tumor, stromal, and immune compartments, uncovered tumor-adjacent populations, and detected cell type-specific spatially variable genes missed by other methods. In mouse embryo and liver cancer, it leveraged context-specific references to resolve organ-specific cell types and increase sensitivity for biologically relevant pathways. Together, these results establish SWIMR as a robust framework for multi-reference deconvolution in spatial transcriptomics.

works.title: Learning Constraints in Protein Evolution beyond Known Substitution Frequencies
works.abstract: During the evolution of protein sequences, amino acid substitutions follow broad patterns that are well established, such as those induced by the physico-chemical properties of residues or the position of sites along the sequence. While these deviations from random changes have been exploited for practical applications, such as to simulate protein evolution or to score protein alignments, they are too general to predict the precise evolution of individual protein sequences. To investigate whether protein sequences contain contextual information about their subsequent evolution beyond that captured by conventional substitution statistics and evolutionary conservation, we trained deep learning models based on an Evolutionary Scale Modeling (ESM2) encoder to predict the rate, the position, and the nature of the amino-acid substitutions in the evolution of ancestral sequences and compared their performance to simpler and explainable heuristics. Our results show that predicting the rate of amino acid changes is achieved equally well by deep learning and by using evolutionary information in outgroup sequences. This suggests that the protein sequence does not contain information that significantly improves the predictions for this task. On the opposite, we show that deep learning models predict the position of these substitutions more accurately than statistics-based baselines. Predictions of the nature of substitutions largely outperform baselines, with over 37% accuracy overall. We observe that rapidly evolving sequences are harder to predict, and substitutions preferentially occur between chemically similar amino acids. Interestingly, predictive information is predominantly contained within a local sequence context of 16 residues. These findings indicate that the nature of substitutions in protein evolution is partly governed by predictive rules that remain to be discovered through a more accurate modeling that could describe evolutionary trajectories based on sequence context alone.

works.title: ALMS1 stabilizes the proximal centriole to drive transition zone assembly and ciliogenesis
works.abstract: The human ciliopathy Alström syndrome is caused by mutations in ALMS1. How ALMS1 contributes to cilia function has been unclear. Unlike other ciliopathy-associated proteins, ALMS1 localizes to the proximal end of centrioles, raising the possibility that it contributes to cilia function via a distinct mechanism. We found that, without ALMS1, centrioles are short and frequently break at their proximal ends. Truncated, broken ALMS1 mutant centrioles display reduced microtubule-organizing activity and disrupted centriole linkers. Without ALMS1, Golgi-derived cargos, including transmembrane components of the transition zone, are impaired in their trafficking to the centrosome. Consequently, ALMS1 is important for transition zone assembly, ciliogenesis, and the control of ciliary membrane composition. In mice, disruption of ALMS1 causes progressive, age-dependent loss of cilia in tissues affected in Alström syndrome, including retina, kidney, and brain. We conclude that Alström syndrome is caused by disruption of proximal centriole integrity and centrosome-directed protein trafficking, compromising ciliary assembly and maintenance.

works.title: An SMN2 splicing-correcting antisense oligonucleotide promotes gene looping and transcription activation
Hierarchical buffering of cellular RNA polymerase II pools maintains transcriptional homeostasis
works.abstract: RNA polymerase II (RNA Pol II) abundance and transcriptional output are coordinated across diverse conditions to maintain mRNA homeostasis. To determine whether RNA Pol II acts as a limiting factor for transcription, we combined acute perturbations with quantitative single-cell imaging and genome-wide profiling. We find that transcription remains stable across 70%-160% of normal RNA Pol II levels in human cells. This robustness emerges from hierarchical buffering mechanisms operating on distinct timescales. Within tens of minutes of monoallelic depletion of RNA Pol II subunit POLR2A, cells maintain steady transcriptional output by drawing polymerases from a nucleoplasmic reserve pool. However, over hours, cellular RNA Pol II holoenzyme levels also recover, driven by constitutive excess POLR2A subunit production rather than feedback sensing. Together, these results reveal that transcriptional homeostasis in human cells is maintained without feedback regulation of polymerase levels, emerging instead from intrinsic kinetics of the multi-checkpoint transcription cycle and holoenzyme assembly.

works.title: A sequence-encoded promoter-proximal super pause stabilizes an offline RNA polymerase II state
A TORC1-regulated H3K4me reader preserves promoter chromatin stability, and its degradation promotes meiotic remodeling
P-TEFb regulates nucleosome positioning at promoters
The chromatin context differently impacts prime editors and base editors and controls the fidelity and purity of base editing
Ca2+ is an intracellular danger signal promoting STING activation
One pocket, two poses: How sequence context shapes non-additive binding
Myosin heavy-chain 9 executes cuproptosis
ecDNA hubs as intrinsic redox reactors that shield extrachromosomal oncogenes
Bacterial 2′,3′-cGAMP signaling induces membrane splitting in antiphage CBASS immunity
A VIPR that wraps: A triplex biochemistry for next-gen biotechnology
Hidden diversity from transposable element RNAs in cancer
PARP1 hyperactivation uncouples transcription from protein expression through nuclear RNA retention
Nuclear TRiC states captured in situ
works.abstract: The chaperonin T-complex protein ring complex (TRiC) is an essential protein-folding machine in eukaryotic cells. Although its cytosolic role in folding newly synthesized proteins is well established, nuclear TRiC remains less well described. Here, we combined cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET), cross-linking and affinity purification mass spectrometry with AlphaFold3 (AF3)-based structural modeling to examine nuclear TRiC in human cells. We detected intermediates of the TRiC duty cycle in the nucleus and identified several nuclear proteins that bind to TRiC. The respective AF3 models suggest interaction surfaces at the inside of the TRiC chamber. Our findings point toward compartment-specific roles of TRiC and a potential function in maintaining nuclear proteostasis. By data-mining very large datasets, our study establishes that rather low-abundant events can be analyzed by cryo-ET. It thus paves the way toward broader applications.

works.title: Identification and regulation of an ACC1-associated lipogenic metabolon in liver
works.abstract: De novo lipogenesis (DNL) plays a pathogenic role in triglyceride (TG) accumulation in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). Strategies to reduce hepatic steatosis focus on inhibiting enzymes involved in DNL and TG synthesis. Here, we identify a nutrient-responsive, post-translational regulatory mechanism that enhances DNL in mouse liver models and primary rat hepatocytes. Under anabolic conditions, ACC1 interacts with multiple enzymes in the DNL and TG synthesis pathway, supporting the formation of an ACC1-associated lipogenic metabolon. Immunofluorescence and electron microscopy (EM) reveal that ACC1 and associated lipogenic proteins are enriched in lipid droplet (LD)-associated and mitochondria-LD interface regions. In steatotic livers, ACC1-associated lipogenic protein interactions are increased, consistent with enhanced hepatic lipogenesis in MASLD. These studies identify a post-translational mechanism that promotes the spatial coordination of lipogenic enzymes and facilitates substrate channeling to enhance TG synthesis. Disruption of this lipogenic metabolon may provide a therapeutic approach for treatment of MASLD.

works.title: Promoter-proximal pausing enables transcriptional buffering of RNA polymerase II availability
works.abstract: While RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) is essential for transcription, the impact of its cellular abundance on gene regulation has been unclear. By titrating RNAPII levels in HEK293 using the dTAG (degradation tag) system, we demonstrate that even modest depletion induces widespread changes in transcription initiation, promoter-proximal pausing, and elongation, along with alterations in splicing, increased transcriptional readthrough, and impaired cell-cycle progression. Interestingly, genes vary considerably in their sensitivity to reduced RNAPII levels. Notably, genes with strong promoter-proximal pausing are largely resistant, effectively buffering RNAPII loss. Moreover, mRNA output is stabilized by increased transcript half-lives under severe depletion. These findings establish RNAPII abundance as a critical determinant of transcriptional regulation, splicing, and termination and identify promoter-proximal pausing as a central buffering mechanism. We propose that the need to buffer RNAPII fluctuations during growth, differentiation, and in response to cellular cues helped drive the evolution of promoter-proximal pausing.

works.title: Dot1 triggers a conserved ribophagy signal to govern ribosome quality and longevity by methylating Rpl12
The C-terminal tail of the RBR E3 ligase RNF14 defines branched K6/K48 polyubiquitin specificity in ribosomal quality control
works.abstract: Ubiquitination is a post-translational modification involving the conjugation of polyubiquitin chains to target proteins. Ubiquitin forms at least eight linkage types with specific biological functions. The diversity of this ubiquitin code is enhanced by branched ubiquitin chains, where two ubiquitin molecules are linked to a third ubiquitin via different linkage types. The E3 ligase RNF14 regulates ribosomal quality control (RQC) upon ribosomal stalling, inducing ubiquitination and degradation of translational cofactors eEF1A or eRF1. Here, we show that RNF14 forms branched K6/K48 polyubiquitin in vitro and on eRF1 in human cells. Structural and mechanistic characterization and comparison with the yeast ortholog Itt1 show that the unstructured RNF14 C-terminal tail defines chain-type and branching specificity. Our work reveals a rare example of a single E3 ligase forming specifically branched polyubiquitin and places branched K6/K48 polyubiquitin into RQC pathways, thereby opening research avenues in RQC and the physiological functions of branched ubiquitin signals.

works.title: Gut microbiota modulation of regulatory DNA elements revealed by massively parallel functional characterization
RBM33 is a unique m6A RNA-binding protein that regulates ALKBH5 demethylase activity and substrate selectivity
A lysosomal DRAM1-GLUT1-NADPH axis coordinates glucose sensing with metabolic reprogramming
Corrigendum: SOX2 phosphorylation during mitosis limits genomic damage
Corrigendum: Transcriptional programs mediating neuronal toxicity and altered glial–neuronal signaling in a Drosophila knock-in tauopathy model
IsoAPA: a multi-species long-read RNA-seq atlas of isoform-resolved alternative polyadenylation
works.abstract: Genes are often treated as the primary unit of regulation, yet it is transcript isoforms that ultimately execute regulatory output, shaping mRNA stability, localization, and protein production. Alternative polyadenylation (APA) diversifies these outcomes by generating alternative 3' ends. However, existing resources catalogue polyadenylation sites (PASs) primarily as genomic events, obscuring the transcript isoforms on which individual sites are used. Here, we present IsoAPA (https://isoapa.sls.cuhk.edu.hk), a systematically curated database that leverages PacBio and Oxford Nanopore long-read RNA-seq to resolve PASs while preserving their native isoform context. The current release contains over 2.3 million transcript-resolved PAS records from 816 sample groups across 99 species. IsoAPA reveals widespread PAS multiplicity within fixed transcript backbones, with a mean of 2.52 distinct retained PASs per observed transcript in the union across 286 human sample groups. Transcript-level analysis further uncovers PAS usage patterns that are masked by gene-level aggregation, both in PAS diversity and in context-dependent dominant-site usage. By anchoring each terminal site within its assigned transcript model, IsoAPA reframes APA analysis from a gene-centred description of terminal-site usage to an isoform-resolved view of transcript-end regulation.

works.title: Subscription and Copyright Information
Advisory Board and Contents
Trends at 50: a mission that matters
The trans-acting potential of expanded repeat RNA
Fatty acid desaturation controls cellular fate decisions between senescence and ferroptosis
works.abstract: When subject to damage or stress, cells develop responses in order to maintain tissue homeostasis. Two such responses are ferroptosis and cellular senescence, but how cells decide between these outcomes remains unclear. Here, we show that senescent cells increase import and membrane levels of multiple polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), but a specific intermediate PUFA, dihomo-gamma-linolenic acid (DGLA, 20:3ω-6), is reduced. Exogenous repletion of DGLA instead results in cell death by ferroptosis. Senescent cells manifest additional features associated with ferroptosis, including labile iron and expression of lipoxygenases as well as low-level membrane peroxidation. Oral DGLA supplementation lowers markers of senescence in aged mice and improves age-related functional outcomes. Finally, obese humans with lowered DGLA desaturation rates have lower markers of adipose tissue senescence. Together, our data implicate shifts in PUFA metabolism as a driver of decisions between senescence and ferroptosis.

works.title: Industrialization drives convergent microbiome and host physiological shifts in the human metaorganism
works.abstract: Understanding how industrialization reshapes the human metaorganism requires integrating microbiome ecology with host physiology across globally diverse populations. Here, we generate multivariate data from the Global Microbiome Conservancy cohort, including gut microbiome, immunoglobulin A (IgA) sequencing, host genotyping, diet, lifestyle, and fecal biomarker profiles, to investigate host-microbiome interactions across gradients of industrialization and geography. We show that industrialization is associated with homogenized microbial compositions, reduced microbial diversity, and lower community stability, independent of host confounders. We further show that industrialization is linked to elevated markers of gut stress, increased IgA secretion, and altered patterns of IgA-bacteria interactions. Finally, we show that microbiome-based disease predictors trained on industrialized populations are uninformative in less industrialized cohorts, highlighting limited cross-population transferability. Together, our results reveal coordinated restructuring of the microbial ecosystem and host physiology and emphasize the need for inclusive, globally representative data to improve translational microbiome applications across diverse human populations.

works.title: Convergent genomic evolution of human gut bacteria along an industrialization gradient
works.abstract: Whether human-associated environments drive adaptive genome evolution in gut commensal bacteria remains largely unknown. Here, we investigate how genomic adaptation in gut bacteria differs between industrialized and non-industrialized human populations. We generated a collection of isolate genomes spanning diverse host geographies, lifestyles, species, and strains. We first found that, compared with metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), paired isolate genomes recover more functional elements and signals of horizontal gene transfer (HGT). Leveraging isolate genomes from multiple species, we find that strains from industrialized hosts experience an expansion of proteome size and harbor greater pangenome fluidity, driven by recent HGT events. Gene- and variant-level analyses reveal convergent patterns of lifestyle-specific adaptation in functions that are critical for ecological adaptation, such as the stress response, cell-envelope remodeling, and central metabolism. Our results demonstrate that industrialization drives convergent genome evolution in gut bacteria, providing a framework for understanding the mechanisms of microbial adaptation to rapidly changing human environments.

works.title: Single-cell, multi-region profiling of the macaque brain across the lifespan
works.abstract: Brain aging is a complex process with profound health and societal consequences. However, the molecular and cellular pathways that govern its temporal progression-along with any cell type-, region-, and sex-specific heterogeneity in such progression-remain poorly defined. Here, we present a transcriptomic atlas of 5.3 million cells from 582 samples spanning 11 brain regions of 55 rhesus macaques (29 female, 26 male), aged 5 months (early life) to 21 years (late adulthood). We annotate 12 major cell classes and 225 subclusters, including region-specific subtypes of excitatory and inhibitory neurons, astrocytes, and ependymal cells. We identify a vulnerable excitatory neuron population in the superficial cortical lamina and a cortical interneuron population that are less abundant later in life, along with subtle, region-specific, age-associated compositional differences in subpopulations of microglia and oligodendrocytes, whose detection required single-cell resolution. Finally, we chart convergent and divergent age-associated molecular signatures across brain regions and cell classes-where some of these signatures are sex-specific and could underlie sex biases in neurological disorders. We find that age-associated transcriptional programs not only overlap substantially with those seen in Alzheimer's disease (AD), but also unfold along distinct temporal trajectories across brain regions, suggesting that aging and AD may share molecular roots that emerge at different life stages and in region-specific, sex-specific windows of vulnerability. This work provides a temporal, regional, and sex-stratified atlas of the aging primate brain, offering insights into cell type-specific vulnerabilities and regional heterogeneity with translational human relevance.

works.title: Disruption of cell-type-specific molecular programs of striatal spiny projection neurons in autism
Spatial transcriptomics reveals molecular organization of human and nonhuman primate basal ganglia
works.abstract: Abstract The basal ganglia are interconnected subcortical nuclei with complex topographical organization that orchestrate goal-directed behaviors and are implicated in neurodegenerative movement disorders. We generated a cellular-resolution, spatial transcriptomic atlas of the basal ganglia in human, rhesus macaque, and common marmoset, sampling over one million cells in each species. By integrating spatial data with a cross-species, consensus snRNA-seq cell type taxonomy, this atlas reveals conserved principles of molecular organization within and across structures. The cellular architecture is complex but highly stereotyped, with gene expression gradients superimposed onto discrete compartments. Extensive spatial sampling illuminates 3D gradients of molecular organization in the striatum and reveals cell type-specific core and shell compartments in the primate internal globus pallidus, which is conserved with mouse. This unified, cross-species spatial transcriptomic atlas will be a foundational resource for characterizing the molecular and functional organization of the basal ganglia and their roles in health and disease.

works.title: Spatial and regulatory organization of cell identity across the primate subcortex
works.abstract: Mammalian brain cell identity is shaped by intrinsic factors and external context. We present a spatially resolved transcriptomic and gene regulatory atlas of cell types found across all subcortical brain regions in a primate - the marmoset monkey. Dense sampling and cross-species integrations revealed spatially precise neuronal assemblies, including in complex structures such as hypothalamus. We find chromatin accessibility and transcriptional identity are spatially tuned within and across subcortical structures. Spatial gradients within subfields of the hippocampal formation are predominantly orchestrated by graded transcription factors coupled with graded enhancers. The primate-expanded population of GABAergic neurons in the thalamus shares transcriptional and regulatory syntax with neurons in superior colliculus, reflecting an evolutionary adaptation compared with rodents. We show that unexpected transcriptional convergence, such as between striatal GABAergic medium spiny neurons and telencephalic glutamatergic neurons, can arise when distinct gene regulatory networks impinge on the same downstream genes.

works.title: Multiscale spatial atlas of human basal ganglia cell types and communities
works.abstract: SUMMARY We generated a multi-region, subcellular-resolution spatial transcriptomic atlas of the human basal ganglia by integrating MERFISH+ and Stereo-seq across four neurotypical donors. These datasets profiled ∼7 million cells spanning the caudate, putamen, nucleus accumbens, and globus pallidus, resolving 60 transcriptionally distinct cell types. We show region-selective, molecular and spatial diversification of medium-spiny-neuron cell types and multiple non-neuronal populations with distinct molecular identities and spatial localizations. Subcellular RNA localization captures somatic size and projection-inferred signatures that reflect direct and indirect pathway topology. Cellular community analyses reveal the enrichment of sub-clusters of astrocytes and oligodendrocytes at striosome–matrix borders, while primate-expanded interneurons are confined to matrix territories. Cross-species mapping uncovers orthologous striosome–matrix organization and conserved dorsolateral-ventromedial gene expression gradients. This atlas provides a foundational molecular and spatial framework for studying human basal ganglia architecture, offering a multi-centimeter scale resource that links cell types, spatial architecture, and subcellular transcript topography across multiple nuclei. Highlights Our multi-centimeter scale spatial taxonomy identifies the precise locations of 60 neuronal and glial cell types of human basal ganglia. MERFISH+ and Stereo-seq platforms map consistent spatial modules that align with classical neuroanatomical nuclei. D1D2 hybrid MSNs and primate-expanded interneurons show regional and domain specific organization Subcellular RNA localization reports soma morphology and projection-inferred signatures.

works.title: Reconstructing developmental and disease progression with sample-level embeddings
Cross-species multiomic atlas of the primate basal ganglia
works.abstract: The basal ganglia (BG) are conserved brain regions essential for motor control, learning, emotion, and cognition, and are implicated in neurological and psychiatric disease. Yet a unified cross-species taxonomy of BG cell types is lacking, limiting translation of BG circuit mechanisms, interpretation of human genetic risk, and development of cell type-targeted tools. We present a multiomic consensus atlas of 1.8 million nuclei from human, macaque, and marmoset spanning eight BG structures. Integrating cross-species gene expression, open chromatin, and spatial profiling enables definition of conserved and divergent cell types. Alignment to existing mouse and human atlases identifies 61 homologous cell types conserved over 80 million years. We identify a STRd D2 StrioMat Hybrid medium spiny neuron (MSN) type with molecular, electrophysiological, and morphological features that clarify hybrid MSN identities. Comparative cis-regulatory analysis reveals conserved sequence grammars that encode cell identity and inform viral targeting strategies, providing a foundational resource for BG evolution, function, and disease.

works.title: Circuit-aligned specialization of human basal ganglia astrocytes
A single-cell and spatial 3D multi-omic atlas of developing human basal ganglia
works.abstract: The human basal ganglia (BG), subcortical nuclei fundamental to motor regulation and cognitive modulation, is constructed from neurons produced during gestation in the adjacent ganglionic eminences (GEs). GEs are transient structures in the ventral prenatal brain that also generate GABAergic inhibitory neurons which migrate to destinations in the BG, cortex and other destinations. This study aims to elucidate the epigenomic and 3D-genomic dynamics involved in the specification and maturation of GEs and GE-derived neurons, using single-nucleus methyl-3C sequencing (snm3C-seq), highly-multiplexed spatial transcriptomics, and chromatin+RNA single-molecule imaging. Our multi-modal data support a heterogeneous temporal progression across GE subregions, with the lateral GE (LGE) showing declining neurogenic activity in mid-gestation and caudal GE (CGE) exhibiting ongoing developmental progression through infancy. We identified regulatory programs that specify subtypes of BG principal cells, medium spiny neurons (MSN), via synchronized maturation of the 3D-epigenome. In infant brains, we found a transient short-range enriched (SE) chromatin conformation during the transition between oligodendrocyte progenitors (OPCs) and oligodendrocytes (ODCs), and a temporary shift toward Long-range Enriched (LE) chromatin conformation in projection neurons, extending previous works showing the differentiation of neurons and glial cells is associated with permanent SE and LE conformation, respectively. Lastly, we found that gene regulatory regions active in MSNs were enriched in loci associated with genetic risk for neuropsychiatric disease. Our study delineates the highly complex, lineage-specific 3D genomic dynamics in ventral progenitors and basal ganglia populations of the perinatal human brain.

works.title: CRISPR mutagenesis of the MYC locus reveals a druggable ultraconserved RNA element
Single-cell multimodal atlas reveals regulatory programs in the human brain
works.abstract: SUMMARY Directly measuring chromatin states alongside transcription is essential for understanding how cell-type-specific regulatory programs are established and maintained in the adult human brain. We present a large-scale single-cell multimodal atlas generated by jointly profiling transcriptome with active (H3K27ac) and repressive (H3K27me3) histone modifications across 18 brain regions. We profile >750,000 nuclei spanning 160 cell types and integrate these data with chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, 3D genome architecture, and spatial transcriptome. This framework annotates >500,000 regulatory elements and resolves cell-type-specific chromatin states. We link enhancers to target genes, infer gene regulatory networks, and classify chromatin interactions, revealing neuron-enriched long-range Polycomb repression of developmental genes. Integrating these maps with GWAS data and sequence-based model prioritizes noncoding variants, effector genes, and vulnerable cell types for neuropsychiatric disorders. Finally, cross-species comparisons show conserved activation but more divergent repression. Together, this study provides a functional reference for interpreting noncoding variants, epigenetic memory, and brain organization. HIGHLIGHTS Joint single-cell profiling of transcriptomes with active or repressive histone modification in >750,000 nuclei across adult human brain. Chromatin state annotation of >500,000 candidate cis -regulatory elements distinguishes active enhancers from accessible and Polycomb-repressed regions. Cell-type-resolved regulatory networks and sequence-based deep learning model prioritize functional neuropsychiatric risk variants. Spatial epigenomic imputation reveals laminar layer-specific Polycomb repression programs. Integration with 3D genome architecture reveals neuron-specific super long-range chromatin loops silencing early developmental genes. Evolutionary analysis uncovers conserved active regulatory grammar but divergent repressive landscape.

works.title: Single-cell analysis of chromatin state and transcriptome in the human basal ganglia
works.abstract: SUMMARY The basal ganglia play essential roles in motor control, emotion, learning and reward processing. Their dysfunction contributes to many neurological and psychiatric disorders. However, the gene regulatory programs defining basal ganglia cell-type identity and function remain poorly understood, limiting interpretation of disease-associated non-coding variants. Here, we present the first single-cell multiome atlas of histone modifications and transcriptomes across eight basal ganglia regions from neurotypical adult human donors. Joint profiling reveals cell-type-specific deployment of active and repressive cis -regulatory elements and gene regulatory networks, and suggests a combinatorial homeobox transcription factor code underlying cell identity. Integration with matched spatial transcriptomic MERFISH data uncovers regional heterogeneity of epigenomic landscapes. Comparative analysis between human and mouse medium spiny neurons uncovers conservation of core gene regulatory features. This atlas interprets non-coding risk variants of neuropsychiatric disorders and supports the development of a deep learning model to predict gene regulation and functional effects of disease-associated variants. HIGHLIGHTS Joint single-cell profiling of transcriptomes and three histone modifications across eight human basal ganglia regions characterizes active and repressive chromatin states at cell-type resolution. Cell-type-specific gene regulatory programs decode combinatorial homeobox TF grammar governing the identity and diversification of basal ganglia neurons. Intergrative analyses link noncoding neuropsychiatric risk variants to specific cell types, regulatory elements, and candidate target genes. A sequence-to-function deep-learning model predicts gene regulation from DNA sequence and prioritizes functional disease-associated variants.

works.title: An integrative single-cell epigenomic atlas annotates the regulatory genome of the adult mouse brain
works.abstract: SUMMARY Histone modifications underpin the cell-type-specific gene regulatory programs that drive the remarkable cellular diversity of the mammalian brain. Here, we jointly profiled four histone modifications and the transcriptome in 2.5 million nuclei from the adult mouse brain. By integrating these data with chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, and three-dimensional genome organization, we constructed a unified epigenomic atlas spanning over 100 brain cell subclasses, and assigned active, primed, and repressive chromatin states across 81% of the genome. Active chromatin states marked by combinatorial histone modifications better nominate candidate enhancers with functional support than chromatin accessibility alone, while H3K27me3- and H3K9me3-marked chromatin states delineate distinct modes of cell-type-specific gene repression. Finally, this multimodal resource enables deep learning models that predict cell-type-specific epigenomic features and gene expression from DNA sequence, providing a comprehensive framework for annotating the brain regulatory genome and interpreting non-coding disease risk variants. HIGHLIGHTS - A single-cell epigenome atlas of transcription and four histone modifications across 2.5M mouse brain cells - Multimodal integration maps chromatin states across ∼81% of the adult mouse brain genome - Cell-type-resolved chromatin landscapes reveal regulatory programs mediated by enhancers, Polycomb and H3K9me3 - Deep learning models predict cell-type-specific epigenomic features and gene expression from DNA sequence

works.title: Multimodal single-cell epigenomic and 3D genome atlas of the human basal ganglia
works.abstract: Abstract The basal ganglia (BG) underlie motor control, reward processing, and many neurological and psychiatric disorders, but a comprehensive epigenomic and 3D-genome atlas of the human BG is lacking. Here we present a multimodal single-cell atlas profiling DNA methylation and 3D chromatin conformation in 261,331 nuclei (snm3C-seq) across eight subregions, resolving 12 classes, 31 subclasses, and 59 groups. Harmonized under the HMBA basal-ganglia consensus taxonomy, this atlas integrates with matched RNA, ATAC-seq, and histone-modification data across five regulatory layers. We identify millions of cell-type- and region-specific differentially methylated regions enriched for distinct transcription factor motifs and link them to disease-associated heritability. Neuron-specific loops dominate cell-type-specific 3D contact remodeling, while most non-neuron-specific loops are constitutive. Among spiny projection neurons (SPNs), chromatin loops, rather than TAD boundaries, distinguish D1, D2, and eccentric SPN subclasses, with eccentric SPNs showing the most loop-level reorganization among the three. We characterize STR D2 SMYD2-HTR7 SPN, a newly recognized POU6F2⁺ D2-SPN subtype, and reveal region-specific methylation and contact gradients of disease-associated genes, including CADM1 and PDE8B. Integrative gene-regulatory networks reconstruct cell-type-resolved enhancer-promoter links to interpret Parkinson’s disease risk variants at SNCA. Finally, MERFISH spatial profiling combined with cross-species Patch-seq identifies non-SPN neuronal subtypes, including a MOXD1⁺ striosomal STR FS PTHLH-PVALB GABA subtype with distinct electrophysiology, partitioning across the striatal matrix-striosome boundary. Highlights A multimodal single-cell atlas maps DNA methylation and 3D genome architecture across human basal ganglia cell types and subregions. Neuron-specific loops dominate cell-type-specific 3D contact remodeling in the human BG, whereas most non-neuron-specific loops are constitutive. Spiny Projection Neuron (SPN) subtypes exhibit regionally organized epigenomic and 3D genome signatures that align with dorsal-ventral identities. Chromatin loops are the primary distinguishing feature among D1, D2, and eccentric SPN subclasses, with eccentric SPNs being the most 3D-reorganized. Integrated regulatory maps link cell-type-specific enhancers to disease-associated genetic risk in the human basal ganglia. Non-SPN interneurons differ in distribution and in transcriptional and epigenetic identity across the matrix-striosome boundary.

works.title: Morphoelectric diversity and specialization of primate striatal neuron types
works.abstract: The basal ganglia are evolutionary ancient subcortical nuclei that form interconnected loops with the neocortex and limbic system to regulate movement, learning, habit formation, emotion, and motivation. Their dysfunction contributes to major neurological and psychiatric disorders, yet most cellular-level insights derive from rodent studies, leaving knowledge gaps in humans and translationally relevant primate species. To address this, we generated multi-modal Patch-seq data linking transcriptomic identity with morphological and electrophysiological properties in macaque striatum, the input nucleus of the basal ganglia. We found underappreciated diversity among medium spiny neurons, including non-canonical types, and variation aligned with functional gradients. Interneurons also exhibited spatial variation and even greater morphoelectric diversity, highlighting their functional modularity. Despite broad evolutionary conservation, we identified primate-specific features and key differences from rodent striatal neurons. By integrating molecular classification with cellular properties that shape network function, our findings provide insights into the functional organization of the primate striatum.

works.title: Mesoscale molecular architecture of the striatum across cell types and adult aging
works.abstract: The human striatum is a central hub for a diverse array of motor, cognitive, and affective behaviors, yet it lacks obvious cytoarchitectural boundaries that define functional territories. Here, we uncover a robust and molecularly defined mesoscale architecture in the human striatum. Using Slide-tags, a scalable single-nucleus spatial transcriptomics technology, we profiled 1.1 million cells across the full span of the anterior striatum of 19 postmortem donors, spatially mapping all striatal populations. Our data uncover a natural subdivision of the striatum into six zones, each defined by molecularly distinct populations of medium spiny neurons, and featuring spatially coordinated neuron-astrocyte signaling. Relative to MSNs in ventral zones, MSNs in dorsal zones exhibit higher expression of genes for synaptic remodeling and plasticity via ephrin and TGF-beta, while the ventral zone is defined by greater expression of semaphorin, protein chaperone, and hedgehog signaling pathways. By imputing zonal identities onto a larger single-nucleus RNA-seq cohort of 131 donors, we find that the dorsal zones exhibit greater age-related transcriptional changes, and that overall, the gene-expression differences that define spatial zonation patterns are attenuated with advancing age. This atlas provides a mesoscale molecular definition of human striatal anatomy, linking cell type identity to functional specialization and aging susceptibility.

works.title: Common variation of cell abundances and gene expression in the human striatum
works.abstract: The human brain varies from person to person in ways that shape behaviors and vulnerabilities, yet the cellular and molecular bases for inter-individual variation are largely unknown. Here we describe an analysis of cellular and gene-expression variation in four key structures of the striatum complex - the caudate, putamen, nucleus accumbens, and internal capsule - as well as the prefrontal cortex, from single-nucleus RNA-seq analysis of 3.9 million nuclei from 178 adult brain donors. We found that people with more astrocytes in any one brain region tended to have this property in all brain regions sampled; the same was true of striatal interneurons, microglia, and oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs). OPCs showed attrition with age, declining in numbers by approximately 40% between age 30 and age 80 in both gray matter and white matter regions. We identified thousands of age-associated (but few sex-associated) variations in gene expression; the vast majority of these effects of age were cell-type-specific. Aging most strongly affected gene expression in projection neurons - especially striatal medium spiny neurons (MSNs/SPNs) - and had a much smaller effect on gene expression in interneurons. Individuals' ages could be predicted to within about five years based on RNA-expression patterns from any of the striatal cell types. Common genetic variants detectably affected the expression levels of some ten thousand genes; the great majority of these effects were cell-type-specific. These data will provide a foundation for exploring natural inter-individual variation, aging, and tissue-based studies of human brain vulnerabilities.

works.title: Subsistence transition preceded population turnover in the eastern Colombian Andes
Harmonized brain ontology and 3D atlases for human, macaque, and marmoset basal ganglia
works.abstract: SUMMARY A major goal of the BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN) is to create a suite of foundational reference cell atlases and associated standards for human and non-human primate brains. Central to this goal is the creation of cross-species harmonized cellular taxonomies and structural parcellations with formal ontologies that can be mapped into 3D reference frameworks bridging neuroimaging and cellular and histological resolutions. We describe here an iterative approach, focused initially on the basal ganglia, to co-create structural and cellular ontologies in human, macaque and marmoset brains, including a Harmonized Ontology of Mammalian Brain Anatomy (HOMBA), and to map and refine structural parcellations into neuroimaging-based common coordinate frameworks. These references provide the framework for documenting and mapping all experimental sampling in BICAN, allowing analyses of cellular and molecular variation as a function of topographic position, and enabling comparisons of cellular, molecular and neuroimaging-based functional variation within and between primate species. Highlights A hierarchical Harmonized Ontology of Mammalian Brain Anatomy (HOMBA) covering 2348 structures HOMBA-annotated 3D common coordinate frameworks (CCFs) of the basal ganglia across species Histologically informed 3D parcellation/atlas of 280 human subcortical structures indexed by HOMBA Mapping and integration of structural, cellular and functional data with HOMBA and CCFs

works.title: TECR palmitoylation triggers a necrotic cell death program driving acute liver injury
Nicotianamine-driven nickel transport to sink organs underpins maize productivity
COP1 is a temperature-responsive switch in Arabidopsis
works.abstract: Temperature is molecular motion, but how living systems sense this is poorly understood. Many responses in plants integrate light and temperature signals, for example, via light receptors and the circadian clock. CONSTITUTIVE PHOTOMORPHOGENESIS 1 (COP1) regulates light signaling and is necessary for responding to temperature. We show that COP1 acts as a temperature-dependent switch, becoming activated by a warm temperature-induced conformational change. An intramolecular Val-Pro (VP) motif binds to the active site of COP1 at low temperatures, preventing substrate docking. At warmer temperatures, the VP motif becomes detached, enabling client proteins to bind and be degraded. This discovery explains how plants are able to obtain a precise readout of temperature within a given climate range. Altering the binding of the VP motif is sufficient to adjust the temperature range within which the plant responds. This helps us understand how plants are able to adapt to different climates.

works.title: The blood-brain barrier imports diverse neuroprotective proteins through pathways impaired early in Alzheimer’s disease models
works.abstract: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) has been defined primarily by what it excludes, yet the scale and function of physiological blood-to-brain protein transport remain largely unknown. Using bioorthogonal proteomics, we find that the healthy BBB samples 191 plasma proteins and permits 92 into the brain parenchyma. Enriched for carrier and metabolic functions, these proteins home to distinct brain cell types, such as apolipoprotein A1 (APOA1) to astrocytes and alpha-1 antitrypsin (SERPINA1) to microglia. This cell-type tropism relies on a BBB-parenchyma receptor hand-off: APOA1 crosses the BBB via SR-B1 and engages astrocytic ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1), a key Alzheimer's risk gene, driving cholesterol efflux that supports synapse integrity. Unlike LPS-induced nonspecific leakage, early-stage 5xFAD mice show selective BBB transport remodeling, with reduced APOA1 and increased SERPINA1 uptake. Hepatic APOA1 overexpression restores APOA1 in the 5xFAD brain, rescuing astrocytic, synaptic, and behavioral deficits. These findings recast the BBB as a selective interface that recruits neuroprotective circulatory proteins for brain health.

Microcephaly-causative ASPM mutations disrupt mitotic spindle orientation and timely specification of human outer radial glia cells
works.abstract: Mutations in the gene abnormal spindle-like, microcephaly-associated (ASPM) are the most common cause of primary microcephaly (MCPH). The mechanisms underlying MCPH have remained unclear, as ASPM disruption leads to species-specific phenotypes. Using human cortical organoids, we observed premature mitotic spindle randomization in ASPM-mutant ventricular cortical progenitors, followed by their early delamination to the basal compartment. Similar delamination following mitotic spindle misorientation could be induced by overexpression of Inscuteable, further linking the two phenotypes. Delaminated progenitors resembled outer radial glial cells (oRGCs), which are selectively amplified in human corticogenesis, but they failed to adopt a bona fide oRGC identity, displaying downregulation of key oRGC genes required for their amplification and maintenance. Our findings link the evolutionarily conserved requirement of ASPM for proper mitotic spindle orientation to the species-specific timing of delamination and proper specification of human oRGC, shedding light on the origins of species-specific vulnerability to ASPM mutations.

works.title: Coupling of cell proliferation to the segmentation clock promotes robust somite scaling
works.abstract: How developing tissues coordinate growth and patterning to maintain their proportions remains unclear. During vertebrate somitogenesis, somite size scales with the presomitic mesoderm (PSM), where morphogen gradients and oscillating Notch, Wnt (wingless and Int-1), and fibroblast growth factor (FGF) signaling regulate segmentation. We find that proliferation is uniformly distributed throughout the oscillating PSM and, using long-term single-cell tracking and microfluidic entrainment in mouse embryo tails, provide evidence for functional coupling between cell-cycle progression and the segmentation clock, likely involving periodic cyclin D1 regulation among other mechanisms. A minimal model suggests that this coupling promotes uniform PSM growth and morphogen dilution, supporting robust somite formation. Loss of clock function increases Mesp2 patterning irregularity, whereas inhibiting proliferation alters morphogen profiles and somite scaling. Human in vitro somitogenesis models show a comparable clock-cell-cycle phase relationship, suggesting conservation across species. Together, these findings link clock-coupled proliferation to coordinated tissue growth, robust patterning, and scaling.

Trends at 50: a mission that matters
Decoding the functional specificity of E2F3 isoforms
works.abstract: E2F3 is a central regulator of cell cycle progression, development, differentiation, and oncogenesis. Alternative promoter usage generates two major homologous isoforms, E2F3A and E2F3B, differing only at their N-termini. Although E2F3A is traditionally considered an activator and E2F3B a repressor of transcription, studies suggest that both isoforms have overlapping and isoform-specific functions, shaped by differences in temporal expression, protein stability, and target gene specificity. In this review, we examine how E2F3A and E2F3B contribute to proliferation, differentiation, and cancer. We also discuss contradictions and limitations in experimental approaches that have complicated the interpretation of these functions. Finally, we explore how clarifying these roles could help resolve long-standing questions in cell cycle regulation, differentiation, and cancer, where E2F3 plays a major role.

works.title: A tug-of-war in the niche: balancing forces to preserve stemness
Subscription and Copyright Information
Advisory Board and Contents
The Five Phases of cancer cells
works.abstract: Beyond identifying individual malignant hallmarks, the central challenge in cancer biology is to uncover the fundamental organizing principles that underlie the interactive nature of cancer cell behavior. Here, we transform the ancient Wuxing theory into a mechanistically grounded, hypothesis-generating biological framework that conceptualizes cancer cell biology around five mutually interacting processes: Pliability, Hybridity, Aggressivity, Sociability, and Evolutivity (PHASE). By engaging in the circuit of mutual promotion and restriction, these phases form an integrated regulatory system that provides a rationale for organizing diverse malignant properties. Within this framework, cancer traits emerge as context-dependent manifestations of the proposed core interactions. Collectively, PHASE offers a complementary perspective for understanding disease progression that could advance interaction-guided therapeutic strategies to target human cancers.

works.title: Noncanonical metabolic and immune checkpoint topography in cancer
Directional cell motility facilitates side branching in the mammary epithelium in a tension-sensitive manner
works.abstract: Branching morphogenesis is a fundamental developmental process that shapes the architecture of many epithelial organs, including the mammary gland. In essence, it enables epithelia with cylindrical geometry to grow in a tree-like pattern through repeated cycles of elongation and branching. In the mammary gland, branches form by tip splitting (bifurcation) and budding from the stalk (side branching). Here, we utilize 3D confocal time-lapse imaging of ex vivo cultured embryonic mammary glands and a variety of mouse models, to elucidate, for the first time, how side branches form in the mammary epithelium. Our results show that branch formation is preceded by outward directional cell migration, whereas cell divisions or their orientation have a more minor contribution. We also demonstrate that frequency of branching increases substantially upon relaxation of epithelial actomyosin network, induced by deletion of Myh9. Interestingly, mosaic Myh9 ablation impedes cell movement amongst neighbors with higher contractility, whereas complete Myh9 ablation enhances cell movement, suggesting that balancing of non-muscle myosin II-generated forces are needed for effective collective migration.

works.title: Cell scientist to watch – Jonathon Nixon-Abell
works.abstract: Jonathon Nixon-Abell is an Assistant Research Professor in Clinical Neurosciences at the Cambridge Institute for Medical Research, UK. Jonathon studied neuroscience at University College London (UCL) and pursued his PhD in molecular neuroscience through a joint programme between UCL, with Kirsten Harvey, and the National Institutes of Health (NIH), USA, with Craig Blackstone. At the NIH, a collaboration with Jennifer Lippincott-Schwartz to study how endoplasmic reticulum structure is affected by mutations associated with Parkinson's disease introduced him to cell biology and advanced imaging methods. Jonathon subsequently joined Jennifer's lab at the Janelia Research Campus as a postdoc and later returned to the UK to gain expertise in in vitro reconstitution in Peter St George-Hyslop's group at the University of Cambridge. He opened his own lab at Cambridge in 2024, where he investigates organelle communication and dynamics in neurons in health and disease using a range of advanced and super-resolution imaging modalities. For our Special Issue on Imaging Cell Architecture and Dynamics, we spoke to Jonathon about how a fascination with the brain led him to biology, how advancements in imaging technologies are unlocking quantitative neuronal cell biology, and his molecular gastronomy hobby.

works.title: Cell scientist to watch – Meghan Driscoll
works.abstract: Meghan Driscoll is an Assistant Professor at the University of Minnesota in the Department of Pharmacology. A physicist by training, she obtained a PhD from the University of Maryland with Dr Wolfgang Losert working on microfabricated structures. During this project, she began studying the dynamics of cells as they interact with these structures, leading her towards microscopy image analysis. Meghan then went on to join Gaudenz Daunser's lab at the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center as a postdoctoral researcher, where she was able to further develop her expertise in image analysis and 3D cell dynamics. In 2022, she moved to Minnesota to start her own lab, where she continues to use interdisciplinary approaches to understand how geometry influences cell dynamics and signalling. For our Special Issue on Imaging Cell Architecture and Dynamics, we spoke to Meghan about her journey from physics to cell biology, working in an interdisciplinary field, and how principles from playground design and architecture can influence image analysis software.

works.title: An interview with Guest Editor Giulia Zanetti
works.abstract: Giulia Zanetti is a Professor of Structural Biology at Birkbeck College and University College London (UCL), currently seconded to the Francis Crick Institute in London, UK. Her PhD at Oxford University sparked her interest in cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET), where she used the technique to study viral glycoproteins. Continuing working with cryo-ET, she then went on to pursue a postdoc position with Randy Schekman at the University of California, Berkeley, USA, to study coat proteins involved in exit from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). Giulia started her own lab in London in 2014 as part of the Birkbeck-UCL joint Institute of Structural and Molecular Biology between Birkbeck College and University College London and the lab moved to the Crick in 2023. Her lab's research continues to focus on trafficking and cargo exit from the ER using a combination of biochemical approaches and fluorescence and electron microscopy. Giulia is a Guest Editor for the 2026 Journal of Cell Science Special Issue on ‘Imaging Cell Architecture and Dynamics’. We caught up with her to learn more about her career, research interests and experience as a Guest Editor.

works.title: First person – Claire Ortmann de Percin Northumberland
works.abstract: First Person is a series of interviews with the first authors of a selection of papers published in Journal of Cell Science, helping researchers promote themselves alongside their papers. Claire Ortmann de Percin Northumberland is first author on ‘In situ visualization of autophagy reveals the presence of vesicles at the expanding phagophore rim’, published in JCS. Claire conducted the research described in this article while a PhD student in Prof. Dr Carsten Sachse's lab at the Ernst-Ruska Centre for Microscopy and Spectroscopy with Electrons, Jülich, Germany. She is now a Postdoc in the lab of Prof. Dr Maria Rosenthal at Bernhard-Nocht Institut for Tropical Medicine, Hamburg, Germany investigating molecular and cellular structures and elucidating them using a range of methods, including cryogenic electron microscopy in its various different flavours.

works.title: Making smart microscopy deployable in imaging core facilities
works.abstract: Smart microscopy, in which real-time image analysis enables microscopes to adapt their acquisition dynamically, is becoming central to biological imaging. However, deploying such workflows in imaging facilities remains challenging. The computers that control microscopes in a facility are shared, governed by institutional policies, often offline and run vendor-specific software. As a result, installing custom software environments for the workflow of each user is both unsafe and unsustainable. We argue that smart microscopy requires a practical deployment strategy that links open-source bioimage analysis with commercial acquisition software without turning acquisition computers into development platforms. Using our recently developed tools, NucleiSky and LabConstrictor, as examples, we demonstrate how microscope control and external image analysis can be integrated while keeping the custom Python environment separate from the vendor-managed environment. The deployment strategy might vary - for instance, a USB drive, a facility workstation, a server or a network share - but the underlying principle remains the same: smart-microscopy workflows must be straightforward to approve, launch, reuse, audit and remove. Smart microscopy will become routine only when it is both powerful and deployable.

works.title: First person – Fabiola Campestre
works.abstract: First Person is a series of interviews with the first authors of a selection of papers published in Journal of Cell Science, helping researchers promote themselves alongside their papers. Fabiola Campestre is first author on ‘Analysis of motor-based transport in primary cilia by dynamic mode decomposition of live-cell imaging data’, published in JCS. Fabiola conducted the research described in this article while a PhD student and postdoc in Lotte Bang Pedersen's lab at Department of Biology, University of Copenhagen, Denmark. She is interested in how cells organize molecular transport and signaling to build and maintain sensory structures like primary cilia.

Quiñones-Frías at Bates College, Lewiston, with a research goal of uncovering the neuron-specific functions of the endoplasmic reticulum and other membrane trafficking pathways.

works.title: First person – Sophie Huver
works.abstract: First Person is a series of interviews with the first authors of a selection of papers published in Journal of Cell Science, helping researchers promote themselves alongside their papers. Sophie Huver is first author on ‘ Live-cell imaging of inter-organelle contacts using an integrated dimerization-dependent fluorescent protein reporter’, published in JCS. Sophie conducted the research described in this article while a PhD student in Catherine Tomasetto's lab at Institut de Génétique et de Biologie Moléculaire et Cellulaire (IGBMC), France.
