Her research interests focus on cell biology, inter-organelle communication and the development of cellular models and tools to better understand these processes.

works.title: First person – Scott Brooks
works.abstract: First Person is a series of interviews with the first authors of a selection of papers published in Journal of Cell Science, helping researchers promote themselves alongside their papers. Scott Brooks is first author on ‘ CelFDrive – multimodal deep learning-assisted microscopy for automated detection of rare events’, published in JCS. Scott is an AI Engineer/Knowledge Transfer Partnership Associate (Smart Microscopy Developer) in the lab of Prof. Andrew McAinsh and Prof. Till Bretschneider at Warwick Medical School, UK, where he develops deep-learning computer-vision methods that allow microscopes to identify and respond to biological events as they happen.

works.title: Single-cell size and growth measurements at a glance
works.abstract: The cell, the basic unit of life, can range over 13 orders of magnitude in volume between species. The size of a cell sets its maximum biosynthetic capacity, molecular content and physical properties. Cell size measurements can inform research into cell growth, the cell cycle and physiology, and are used to describe disease states and guide physical and ecological models. However, measuring size - and its dynamic increase, growth - is technically challenging, and data interpretation depends on the technology used. This Cell Science at a Glance article and the accompanying poster summarize the key methods for measuring single-cell volume or dry mass. The performance, potential biases and convenience of each method are discussed to guide experimental setup and interpretation. In addition, technological limitations and the need for future collaborative efforts are highlighted.

works.title: Live-cell imaging of inter-organelle contacts using an integrated dimerization-dependent fluorescent protein reporter
works.abstract: Organelles communicate with each other by building membrane contact sites (MCSs) via specialized protein-protein and/or protein-membrane interactions. Conventional light microscopy cannot distinguish organelles connected by MCSs from those merely juxtaposed. In addition, organelle contacts are dynamic, yet only a limited number of tools are available to monitor MCSs in living cells. In this study, we developed a series of reporters based on dimerization-dependent fluorescent proteins (ddFP) to visualize, quantify and follow inter-organelle contacts. We first generated an integrated system specifically designed to study contacts between late endocytic compartments (late endosomes and lysosomes) and the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). This system utilizes a single plasmid coding for the two complementary ddFP components: green A (GA) and green B (GB) targeted to the ER and late endosomes and lysosomes (LE/Lys), respectively. This construct enabled the generation of a stable reporter cell line suitable for semi-quantitative imaging. The ddFP reporter, which we called ddFP LELYS-ER, did not perturb endogenous LE/Lys-ER contacts in stable cells, and detected changes in the number of LE/Lys-ER contacts, for example, upon downregulation of the ER-resident VAP tether protein family, or under conditions of lysosomal damage. Moreover, live-cell imaging revealed that LE/Lys-ER contacts have distinct shapes, mobilities and lifetimes. Finally, using the same vector design, we generated two additional integrated reporter systems adapted to the study of contacts between the ER and the plasma membrane, and between the ER and mitochondria.

works.title: First person – Chih-Hsuan Hsu
works.abstract: First Person is a series of interviews with the first authors of a selection of papers published in Journal of Cell Science, helping researchers promote themselves alongside their papers. Chih-Hsuan Hsu is co-first author on ‘Tubulin polyglutamylation modulates Golgi morphodynamics and neurite branching during neuronal morphogenesis’, published in JCS. Chih-Hsuan is a PhD student in the lab of Sarah Cohen at The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, USA, studying cellular processes under microscopes to understand how neurons develop their complex architecture.

works.title: How to make microscopy images that are color blind friendly
works.abstract: These days, there is increased awareness about color blindness (also known as color vision deficiency) and figure accessibility. During peer review, referees are now more likely to request changes to color palettes in papers to assist color blind readers. This is a positive change, and of course it is best to check that our images are accessible. However, it is less useful when referees reflexively request changes because they believe that certain color combinations should be 'outlawed' for reasons of accessibility. What I mean is: some scientists believe that all red-green-blue overlays are fundamentally bad for accessibility. In this short Essay, I try to set out why that view is misguided and to provide some practical solutions to the problem.

works.title: Expanding global access to advanced microscopy
works.abstract: Microscopy offers detailed insight into the internal world of cells and has underpinned many fundamental discoveries in cell biology. However, state-of-the-art technology is not only expensive to maintain but requires specialised expertise and physical access to parts, meaning that cutting-edge techniques are not always accessible to all research groups. In this Essay, Journal of Cell Science has invited four researchers to discuss their own perspectives on approaches to democratise microscopy across the world. What are the best distribution strategies to improve access to microscopes and facilities across Africa? How can open-source approaches support local maintenance and development of microscopes in Latin America when hardware access and company support is not always readily available? How can networks help build regional expertise in super-resolution imaging to ensure researchers have the right microscopy support? Finally, the authors explore how the choice of technique itself can enable easier access to high-resolution imaging - by physically enlarging the sample, expansion microscopy reduces the requirement for expensive, specialised microscopes. With increasing strategies to reduce costs and improve resource distribution, advanced imaging techniques and improved resolution are becoming more widely available to support future discoveries in cell biology across the world.

works.title: Beyond the lens – visualizing the wonders of microscopic life with accessible and frugal tools
works.abstract: In the 17th century, the first microscopes revealed an unexpected microbial world that fascinated both the scientific community and the general public. Fast-forward 300 years, and we can now map molecular and cellular architectures in exceptional detail. High-resolution imaging has unveiled a much wider diversity of unicellular organisms, which sustain virtually every ecosystem and are indispensable to human health, with unprecedented visual complexity. However, despite improved observational capabilities and an exponential increase in imaging data available, the general public still has limited direct experience or perception of microbial life. This reveals a crucial gap in our current approaches to scientific communication, which focus on 'telling' rather than 'showing'. In this Essay, we argue that developing accessible and frugal tools that allow anyone to directly experience this wonderful microbial world is essential to deeper public scientific understanding. By sharing design principles of two related initiatives - Foldscope and PlanktoQuest - we highlight the importance of making the invisible world of microorganisms tangible and visible to everyone. Through learning by experience, we demonstrate a unique bottom-up approach for developing aptitude and intuition for the bizarre and wonderful world of microbes so as to bring everyone directly into the visual experience of the microscopic world.

works.title: First person – Houssam Al-Koussa
works.abstract: First Person is a series of interviews with the first authors of a selection of papers published in Journal of Cell Science, helping researchers promote themselves alongside their papers. Houssam Al-Koussa is first author on ‘FRET imaging of ERK activity in an orthotopic xenograft model of patient-derived pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma using imaging window’, published in JCS. Houssam conducted the research described in this article while a PhD student in Dr Toru Hiratsuka's lab at the Graduate School of Biostudies, Kyoto University, Kyoto, Japan. He is now a Research Associate in the lab of Prof. Takaharu Okada at RIKEN Center for Integrative Medical Sciences, Yokohama, Japan, with research interests in intravital imaging, cell signaling and cancer biology.

works.title: First person – Hélène Spangenberg
works.abstract: First Person is a series of interviews with the first authors of a selection of papers published in Journal of Cell Science, helping researchers promote themselves alongside their papers. Hélène is first author on ‘A phosphoinositide and RAB switch controls early macropinocytosis’, published in JCS. Hélène conducted the research described in this article while a PhD candidate/postdoc in Harald Stenmark's and Kay Oliver Schink's lab at Institute for Cancer Research, the Norwegian Radium Hospital, Oslo, Norway. She is now a postdoc in the lab of Kay Oliver Schink at Domus Medica, Oslo, Norway, investigating membrane trafficking and RAB GTPases.

works.title: Resolving new dimensions in cell architecture and dynamics
works.abstract: Advances in microscopy and bioimaging are resolving the fundamental processes of life at ever-finer scales. Improvements in spatial, temporal and molecular resolution, as well as correlative and multiplexed techniques, are converging towards an increasingly clear picture of how cell behaviour and physiology emerge from physicochemical properties, molecular interactions and subcellular architectures. Yet, these advances have also exposed specific challenges to visualising key dimensions of biological structure, function and diversity. For our Special Issue on Imaging Cell Architecture and Dynamics, Journal of Cell Science invited early-career researchers who are tackling these challenges to share their perspectives on pushing the limits of what bioimaging can resolve. The authors discuss how their methods can access new layers of biological function - from in situ mapping of protein structure with conventional microscopes, to multiplexed visualisation of elemental distributions and complex molecular interactions, and super-resolution imaging of cell behaviour at sub-zero temperatures - in unexpected and innovative ways.

works.title: LiSIUM – a light sheet bioimaging hub in South America
works.abstract: Light sheet microscopy has revolutionized biological imaging, yet prohibitive procurement costs and technical demands have restricted its availability in South America, creating a persistent technological gap for regional biomedical research. The Light Sheet Imaging at Universidad Mayor initiative (LiSIUM) has established a framework for regional access, capitalizing on a fully operational, state-of-the-art light sheet platform. In this Essay, we describe the implementation of LiSIUM and its core framework for expanding advanced imaging access across South America. This initiative has built a regional community for knowledge transfer through allocated funding, travel grants, and a structured program of international workshops, specialized courses and technical specialist support. LiSIUM provides a vital platform for high-resolution four-dimensional imaging, particularly for developmental biology, enabling investigators to address fundamental embryological questions ranging from cell fate determination to complex tissue morphogenesis. Ultimately, LiSIUM serves as a scalable model for mitigating technological disparities and empowering the next generation of researchers in resource-constrained scientific communities.

works.title: Imaging cell architecture and dynamics – from images to insight
From intracellular force maps to organelle and organism physiology
works.abstract: The mechanical properties of the cell interior are heterogeneous, varying across components and compartments according to function, location and time. However, many current mechanical models of the cell do not fully reflect this, either treating the cell as a simplified isotropic mechanical continuum or focusing on complex mechanics of isolated cellular structures, leaving the integration of mechanical features at cellular-to-tissue levels unresolved. To link mechanics with biological function, complete, spatially and temporally resolved maps of subcellular to mesoscopic mechanical properties in living systems and organisms are needed. Despite major technical advances in mechanobiology over the past decade, only snapshots of these heterogenous material properties have been obtained. Crucially, the integration of quantitative force measurements with microscopy approaches remains a challenge in connecting cell mechanics with biological structure and function. This limitation underlines the urgent need for novel imaging methods to visualize how different organelles, cells and organisms respond to forces and how their mechanical properties are coupled to function and physiology. In this Review, we outline recent developments in this rapidly advancing field and discuss what lays ahead in order to bring spatially and temporally resolved imaging of subcellular mechanics into a quantitative and broadly accessible framework for cell biology.

works.title: Cell size asymmetry regulates neural stem cell proliferation and lineage expansion in the Drosophila brain
works.abstract: Asymmetrically dividing invertebrate and vertebrate stem cells can produce unequal sibling cell sizes but the function of cell size asymmetry (CSA) remains underexplored. Here, we use Drosophila neural stem cells (NSCs) to investigate how changes in CSA affect cell fate decisions and neurogenesis. Using live-cell imaging, NSC lineage analysis, and gene expression profiling, we find that altering CSA expands the NSC pool but restricts lineage expansion. Ordinary differential equation (ODE) models suggest two possible mechanisms: NSC volume sensitivity and NSC self-inhibition. Consistent with the volume-sensitivity model, the NSC growth regulator Imp and the G1-S cell-cycle regulator CycE are upregulated in NSCs with altered CSA. In addition, the differentiation factor Prospero is asymmetrically inherited in symmetrically dividing NSCs, suggesting a mechanism for NSC self-inhibition. Together, our results suggest that cell size and cell fate determinants regulate NSC proliferation lineage expansion and progeny differentiation in the developing Drosophila brain.

works.title: Mouse APOE Christchurch protects against Aβ-induced tau and α-synuclein aggregation
works.abstract: Apolipoprotein E ( APOE ) genotype alters the risk for Alzheimer's disease (AD) but also affects dementia risk in Parkinson's disease (PD) and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB). Recent evidence suggests that the APOE Christchurch (CC) mutation protects against AD, however, its effects on PD and DLB are unknown. We generated an APOE CC knock-in mouse to understand its effects on amyloid-β (Aβ), tau, and α-synuclein (α-syn) aggregation. APOE CC mice show increased plasma cholesterol and triglyceride levels, decreased Aβ and Aβ-induced tau pathology after intracortical AD-tau injection into 5xFAD mice but do not change Aβ or tau pathology in individual transgenic mouse models without injection. Interestingly, APOE CC reduces formation and spread of α-syn aggregation in the brain, peripheral-to-spinal cord spread, and directly increases binding affinity to α-syn compared to APOE WT. Our study emphasizes the remarkable protective effects of a point mutation in murine APOE against Aβ-induced tau and α-syn aggregation.

works.title: Exposure to immune stimuli augments alveolar macrophages to acquire neutrophil antimicrobial molecules to prevent bacterial pneumonia
works.abstract: The protective adaptation of innate immune defenses against respiratory pathogens has been linked to previous exposure to immune stimuli; however, the underlying mechanisms of these adaptations are not yet fully understood. Here, we show that pre-exposure to a low dose of non-specific immune stimuli or infection protects against subsequent lethal methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) challenge. This enhanced protection concurs with increased alveolar macrophages (AMs) resulting from a self-renewal process in the lungs. Importantly, these AMs are programmed to acquire neutrophil-released antimicrobial enzymes from the extracellular space to clear MRSA, prevent tissue damage, and rapidly restore lung homeostasis. AM function depends on differential gene expression, including expression of the efferocytosis receptor Mer proto-oncogene tyrosine kinase (MerTK) and the anti-apoptotic regulator Bcl-xL. Thus, our data highlight that AMs acquire neutrophil enzymes as an integral component of innate immune adaptation.

works.title: Exosome secretion is required for Sonic Hedgehog dispersal and signal gradient formation in the embryonic limb bud mesenchyme
works.abstract: Carrier-assisted diffusion and cytoneme transport help disperse Hedgehog morphogens across diverse embryonic tissues, yet their relative contributions to patterning mesenchymal tissues remain poorly understood. Here, we combine signaling assays with quantitative microscopy to establish exosome secretion as a major mechanism for Sonic Hedgehog (Shh) dispersal. Using a synchronous release system to visualize Shh trafficking, we demonstrate that Shh traffics through the exosome biogenesis pathway in limb bud mesenchymal cells. Shh-bound exosomes diffuse through extracellular space and also bind and travel along cytonemes, providing two alternative modes of transport. We show that exosome secretion is essential to establish short-range Shh signaling gradients in vitro and contributes to shaping Shh protein gradients in the limb bud in vivo . We propose that exosome-based Shh secretion, combined with different modes of extracellular transport, provides a tunable mechanism to sculpt Shh gradients across different length and time scales.

works.title: Single-cell and spatial characterization of the human pancreas in cystic fibrosis
works.abstract: Cystic fibrosis (CF) causes severely damaged pancreatic morphology and cystic fibrosis-related diabetes (CFRD), but the cellular drivers of CFRD in the pancreas are not understood. Here, we perform single-cell and spatial profiling of 2.04 M cells from 23 non-disease or CF pancreas donors. A high-mucin ductal sub-type had relatively preserved abundance and genomic profiles but altered localization in CF. Changes in inflammatory and fibrotic pathways were driven by crosstalk between immune and pro-fibrotic cells in specific niches. Beta cells had extensive changes in CF, including increased stress responses and evidence for compensatory secretion, that were distinct from those in type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Islets localized near large adipose tissue and collagen in CF had reduced beta cells linked to signaling from adipocytes, macrophages, stellate cells, and high-mucin ductal cells. Overall, our results highlight pancreatic microenvironments of beta cell dysfunction in CF and offer in-roads to preserving beta cells in CFRD.

works.title: Hyperosmotic stress induces rewiring of 3D chromatin interactions
works.abstract: Cells continually face environmental stressors that challenge homeostasis, yet how three-dimensional (3D) chromatin structure contributes to these stress responses remains unclear under hyperosmotic conditions. To investigate this, we map 3D chromatin structure, its molecular drivers, and transcriptional outcomes during sorbitol-induced hyperosmotic stress. Within 1 hour of sorbitol treatment, pre-existing loops and domains collapse, while several hundred de novo sorbitol-induced loops emerge. These loops are punctate, longer-range, and transient. 3D chromatin structure largely returns to baseline conditions by 24 hours. Loop reorganization is consistent across cell types and hyperosmotic stimuli. Sorbitol-induced loops require cohesin but not CTCF, and anchors are enriched at active promoters harboring GC-rich transcription factor motifs. Genes at these anchors show delayed activation following loop formation, consistent with loops acting upstream of transcription. Together, hyperosmotic stress triggers rapid, reversible, CTCF-independent chromatin reorganization that correlates with transcriptional adaptation.

works.title: Human neocortical glutamatergic neurons revealed through multimodal profiling
works.abstract: The human neocortex underlies higher cognition and is the engine of complex thought. Yet our understanding of its neuronal diversity is limited by sparse access to tissue, inconsistent sampling across studies, and a lack of multiple modality data. Although single-cell transcriptomic taxonomies are an important framework for characterizing cell type diversity, transcriptomic information alone cannot reveal the cellular properties that define neuronal computations. To address this, we performed Patch-seq, a method for collecting Morphology, Electrophysiology, and Transcriptomic data from a single neuron. We focused on glutamatergic, neocortical, excitatory neurons, the principal long-range projecting neurons of the cortex, and systematically integrated their morphoelectric features with transcriptomic identity. In combination with spatial transcriptomic data, we interrogated 39 of 42 transcriptomically-defined neuron types with a layer-centric perspective. Morphoelectric properties, such as cortical depth, apical dendrite structure, and excitability clearly distinguish transcriptomic subclasses and support many finer transcriptomic types. Morphoelectric properties are influenced by spatial location in supragranular layers, while deeper layers exhibit greater heterogeneity. Cross-species comparisons reveal conserved subclass organization but pronounced differences in apical dendrite arborization between mouse and human, and surprising similarities between human and macaque. Together, these datasets provide a unified multimodal reference that advances our understanding of human cortical circuitry and establishes a foundation for experimental and computational studies of human brain function and disease.

works.title: Uncoupling hypersensitive cell death response and disease resistance activated by effector-triggered immunity
works.abstract: Effector-triggered immunity (ETI) is frequently accompanied by the hypersensitive response (HR), a localized form of programmed cell death considered closely associated with disease resistance. However, the mechanistic relationship between HR and effective immunity remains incompletely understood. We show that the Arabidopsis cbp60g sard1 double mutant exhibits exaggerated ETI-associated HR while retaining partial resistance to bacterial pathogens, providing a genetically tractable system uncoupling disease resistance from cell death without visible pleiotropic defects. Transcriptome profiling reveals that CBP60g and SARD1 coordinate positive and negative immune regulatory programs, including activation of the Nudix hydrolase NUDT7, a downstream target that partially restrains HR. The incomplete restoration of the mutant phenotype by NUDT7 overexpression suggests that additional CBP60g/SARD1-dependent negative regulators buffer excessive cell death. Our findings demonstrate that hypersensitive cell death is genetically separable from effective disease resistance and reveal how CBP60g/SARD1 coordinates transcriptional networks to balance immunity with protection against self-inflicted damage.

works.title: Enhancer-based AAV approach for selective AADC delivery reduces motor symptoms and dyskinesia in Parkinson’s mouse models
works.abstract: Profound degeneration of dopamine (DA) neurons and reduced DA levels in the brain is recognized as an underlying cause of Parkinson’s Disease (PD). The standard treatment for PD is levodopa (L-DOPA), but its effectiveness wanes over time and prolonged usage can lead to L-DOPA-induced-dyskinesia (LID). An adeno-associated virus (AAV)-based strategy to overexpress aromatic l-amino acid decarboxylase (AADC) in the striatum combined with LDOPA therapy shows promise for symptomatic improvement but requires an invasive delivery approach. Here, we generated enhancer AAVs to drive AADC expression in key cell types and paired them with a blood-brain barrier (BBB)-penetrant capsid. We characterized the AAVs in mouse following multiple routes of administration and found that cell-type specific viral treatment ameliorated motor deficits and LID in PD disease models. This cell type-specific viral rescue strategy showed similar or better phenotypic rescue compared to a ubiquitous targeting approach and improved mortality. Additionally, we characterized the expression of an AAVAADC vector capable of mouse phenotypic rescue in non-human primate (NHP) following two routes of administration. This novel therapeutic strategy in combination with L-DOPA may enable a less invasive and better tolerated approach to treat motor deficits in PD patients.

works.title: ApoE-dependent lipid handling by median eminence microglia supports myelin remodeling and metabolic function
works.abstract: Microglia regulate hypothalamic control of systemic metabolism, but the mechanisms underlying their contribution remain unclear. Here, we identify apolipoprotein E (ApoE)-associated microglial transcriptional states enriched in the median eminence (ME), a brain region involved in sensing peripheral cues and metabolic regulation. These transcriptional states are characterized by programs related to lipid handling, interferon-associated responses, and cellular stress. Consumption of a Western diet (WD) increased microglial lipid accumulation and altered myelin remodeling within the ME, while expression of the human APOE4 isoform exacerbated these changes. Deletion of Apoe altered microglial responses to nutritional stress, supporting a role for ApoE in microglial lipid handling. Finally, activation of liver X receptor using synthetic high-density lipoprotein (sHDL) nanoparticles enhanced microglial lipid-handling programs, improved hypothalamic leptin responsiveness, reduced food intake, and limited weight gain in WD-fed mice. Together, these findings identify ApoE-dependent lipid handling as a key component of adaptive microglial responses to metabolic stress.

works.title: The fungal phosphate starvation regulator CtPHO4 couples nutrient adaptation to host colonization through the effector NFC1
works.abstract: Plant-associated microbes must balance environmental adaptation with virulence and host colonization to survive in fluctuating ecosystems, yet the molecular mechanisms coupling these processes remain poorly understood. Here, we identify the effector NUTRIENT-DEPENDENT FACILITATOR OF COLONIZATION 1 (NFC1) in a conditionally pathogenic Colletotrichum tofieldiae strain, whose expression is tightly regulated by both temperature and phosphate availability. By leveraging plant phosphate starvation response (PSR) mutants and phosphate supplementation, we demonstrate that NFC1 expression is driven by the internal phosphate status of the host. Notably, the fungal PSR regulator CtPHO4 represses NFC1 and colonization during phosphate starvation, while simultaneously activating canonical fungal PSR-related genes. Conversely, under phosphate sufficiency, NFC1 is strongly induced and promotes infection. This host colonization and adaptation machinery is partially conserved in a beneficial C. tofieldiae strain. This study uncovers a molecular link between metabolic adaptation and host colonization, providing a conceptual framework for understanding fungal lifestyle transitions under changing environments.

works.title: HRS dephosphorylation at membrane contact sites promotes sorting within multivesicular endosomes
works.abstract: HRS is a receptor tyrosine kinase substrate and ESCRT machinery component. It enables sorting of ubiquitylated cargo into multivesicular endosomes (MVEs) for lysosomal degradation but also functions in receptor recycling. We show that co-depletion of its ESCRT-0 binding partners, STAM1 and STAM2, recapitulates defects in EGF receptor (EGFR) sorting onto intraluminal vesicles (ILVs) but does not mirror the increased MVE size evident after HRS depletion. Using mutagenesis of the endogenous gene or introduction of APEX2-tagged HRS variants, we find that HRS Y329/334 phosphorylation is dispensable for EGFR sorting and MVE size control. AnnexinA1 mediates ER:endosomal membrane contacts and promotes EGF-stimulated ILV formation. We show that reduced ILV formation on AnnexinA1 depletion is accompanied by increased HRS phosphorylation, likely through reduced HRS dephosphorylation by ER-localised PTP1B. Conversely, Y329/334 mutation renders ILV formation insensitive to AnnexinA1 depletion. Our data suggest that rapid HRS dephosphorylation at ER:MVE contacts promotes efficient ILV formation.

works.title: Metabolic reprogramming by caloric restriction enhances acute phase virological control and reduces chronic inflammation during SIV infection
works.abstract: Nutrient metabolism influences HIV-1 replication, antiviral immunity, and chronic inflammation, yet remains difficult to leverage therapeutically. Using a non-human primate model of HIV-1, we modulated metabolism through caloric restriction (CR). Four months of 30% CR was safe and induced metabolic reprogramming in rhesus macaques. Compared with ad libitum -fed animals, CR reduced gut mucosal CCR5 + CD4 + T cell frequencies. Following SIV infection, CR reduced acute viremia, dampened type I interferon signaling, and enhanced CD8 + T cell cycling in lymphoid tissues. CR-associated protection coincided with glycolytic upregulation, supporting an early reduction in viremia that waned over time. Following antiretroviral therapy, CR limited gastrointestinal immune activation, improved tricarboxylic acid cycle flux, and reduced plasma sCD14 and TNF-related molecules. Blood SIV DNA remained unchanged, suggesting GI inflammation can be decoupled from viral persistence. These findings demonstrate that dietary intervention can limit lentiviral pathology while revealing the temporally constrained nature of glycolysis in supporting antiviral responses.

works.title: IFN-γ coordinates macrophage-mediated inflammatory resolution and matrix remodeling in heart regeneration
works.abstract: Heart regeneration requires coordinated immune responses that support tissue remodeling and myocardial renewal. Here, we identify interferon-γ (IFN-γ) as an injury-responsive regulator of macrophage function during zebrafish heart regeneration. Loss of ifng1 disrupted immune cell dynamics, impaired debris clearance and collagen remodeling, reduced cardiomyocyte (CM) protrusion and proliferation, and delayed scar resolution. Cardiac macrophage transcriptomes revealed altered inflammatory and ECM-remodeling programs, including reduced expression of matrix metalloproteinases and increased tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases ( timp4.3 ) expression. Macrophage-specific blockade of IFN-γ signaling recapitulated key regenerative defects and was associated with similar dysregulation of ECM-remodeling genes. Nanoparticle-mediated timp4.3 silencing reduced its expression in injured adult hearts and FACS-isolated cardiac macrophages, improved collagen remodeling and CM protrusion, and partially rescued CM proliferation and scar resolution in ifng1 mutants. Together, these findings link macrophage IFN-γ signaling to regenerative ECM remodeling and identify Timp4.3 as a functional downstream regulator.

works.title: A genome-wide CRISPR screening identifies targets that drive tolerogenic dendritic cells
works.abstract: Tolerogenic dendritic cells (TolDCs) contribute to immune tolerance and have demonstrated therapeutic potential in early clinical studies of autoimmune diseases. However, the key molecular pathways driving their differentiation and tolerogenic phenotype remain elusive. Here, we investigated the molecular mechanisms underlying the functional status of TolDCs in response to different tolerizing agents and identified CD86 as a consistent and robust marker downregulated in tolerogenic state. CD86 is functionally required for TolDC-mediated suppression of T cell proliferation and cytokine secretion, supporting its use as a surrogate marker of tolerogenic potential. Leveraging CD86 expression as a readout, we performed a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 knockout screen and characterized genes associated with TolDC phenotypes. This approach positions UBE2L6 as a regulator of CD86 expression through modulation of an ISG15-USP18-associated pathway, implicating its involvement in tolerogenic functions. These findings describe therapeutically targetable pathways to promote immune tolerance.

works.title: Succinate promotes multiple myeloma cell proliferation through TCA cycle oxidation
works.abstract: Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell malignancy that develops within the bone marrow. The bone marrow metabolome is altered in myeloma, with implications for malignant cell growth. Here, the impact of elevated bone marrow levels of the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle metabolite, succinate, was interrogated. Succinate was found to promote proliferation of several myeloma cell lines. This was linked to its uptake and oxidation in the TCA cycle, as indicated by increased ATP-coupled mitochondrial respiration and incorporation of succinate-derived carbons into downstream TCA cycle intermediates, which also occurs in primary myeloma cells. Succinate-driven proliferation was dependent upon mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and abrogated by ATP synthase inhibition. Furthermore, interrogation of large-scale transcriptomic data identified that elevated expression of a mitochondrial succinate transporter associates with accelerated disease progression in myeloma, indicating this mechanism may promote plasma cell growth in vivo and highlighting a target for therapeutic intervention.

works.title: 5-Azacytidine incorporation into mRNAs disrupts translation and induces ribosome collisions
works.abstract: 5-Azacytidine (5-AzaC) is a cytidine analog chemotherapeutic widely used to treat myeloid malignancies. Although its activity is primarily attributed to DNA hypomethylation, the majority of 5-AzaC is incorporated into RNA, where its functional consequences are less understood. Here, we show that 5-AzaC treatment of cells leads to inhibition of protein synthesis. Ribo-seq, Disome-seq, and RNA-seq in treated cells exhibit a time-dependent C-to-G conversion in mRNAs. These conversion events are enriched within footprint positions corresponding to the A-site of monosomes or stalled leading ribosomes in a disome complex. Footprints are accumulated at sites with C-rich codons in the A-site, with particular emphasis on the second codon position. Consistent with disome-mediated signaling, 5-AzaC activates ZAK- and GCN2-dependent stress responses. Furthermore, loss of the ribosome-associated quality control factor, ZNF598, sensitizes cells to 5-AzaC. These findings suggest that translation disruption represents an additional layer of 5-AzaC's mechanism of action, alongside its known DNA-mediated effects.

works.title: Proteolytic dissection of eIF4G reveals that closed-loop mRNP formation is dispensable for bulk translation in mammalian cells
works.abstract: The "closed-loop" mRNP, in which the 5′ cap and 3′ poly(A) tail are bridged by eIF4E-eIF4G-PABP interactions, has been proposed to drive efficient translation. Direct rigorous tests of this model in mammalian cells have remained elusive. Using auxin-inducible degrons to acutely deplete eIF4G1, we find that global translation is only partially reduced and recovers without restoration of eIF4G1 levels. We identify eIF4G3 as an underappreciated contributor to basal translation that buffers translational output upon eIF4G1 loss. eIF4G1 mutants reveal that PABP binding by eIF4G1 is dispensable for bulk protein synthesis. Further, PABP depletion has no immediate effect on protein synthesis but instead destabilizes poly(A) mRNA. In contrast, the N-terminal enteroviral cleavage product (2A-cp N ) is a potent, dominant translational repressor that requires both PABP- and eIF4E-binding domains for inhibition. These findings suggest that the eIF4G-PABP closed-loop architecture is not required for productive initiation but may be actively co-opted for translational silencing.

works.title: Plagl2 reprograms adult mouse retinal Müller glia for proliferation and injury-enhanced neurogenic competence
works.abstract: Müller glia (MG) in the adult mammalian retina have long been recognized as a potential endogenous source for the regeneration of lost retinal neurons. However, existing MG reprogramming strategies yield an incomplete regenerative response by favoring either proliferation or neurogenic differentiation. Here, we show that the zinc-finger transcription factor gene Plagl2, previously shown to reactivate quiescent neural stem cells, is sufficient to reprogram adult mouse MG into a progenitor-like state with coupled proliferative and neurogenic competence. Using histology, time-lapse imaging, and single-cell transcriptomics, we find that Plagl2 drives regulated rounds of MG cell cycle re-entry, while N-methyl-D-aspartate-induced retinal injury further promotes the acquisition of neurogenic competence biased toward inner nuclear layer neuronal identities. These findings indicate that Plagl2 regulates mammalian MG reprogramming, and supports a broader approach to tissue regeneration through the adaptation of reprogramming modules across distinct cell types.

works.title: The YAP/TAZ-Tgfbr2-stiffness feedback loop governs divergent cell fates of muscle-resident mesenchymal progenitors
works.abstract: Mesenchymal progenitors are essential for muscle regeneration, but also contribute to fat accumulation and fibrosis. Several extrinsic and intrinsic factors regulating adipogenic or fibrogenic differentiation of mesenchymal progenitors have been identified. However, it remains unclear how different cues are integrated to determine cell fate. Here, we demonstrate that interstitial stiffness and the mechanosensitive hippo pathway regulate mesenchymal progenitor cell fate. Fat accumulation model reduced interstitial stiffness and nuclear YAP/TAZ-positive mesenchymal progenitors compared with a regeneration model, whereas YAP/TAZ deficiency in mesenchymal progenitors enhanced fat deposition. Mechanistically, YAP/TAZ induced expression of the anti-adipogenic genes Aldh1a2 and Wnt5a, and the pro-fibrogenic gene Tgfbr2, which mediates TGF-β binding. Loss of Tgfbr2 in mesenchymal progenitors reduced transient collagen deposition, decreased stiffness, and increased fat accumulation during regeneration. We propose a stiffness-YAP/TAZ-Tgfbr2-collagen regulatory loop governing mesenchymal progenitor cell fate and highlight its importance for optimal muscle regeneration.

works.title: The FERONIA receptor kinase is required for high-humidity responses in Arabidopsis
works.abstract: High humidity greatly influences plant growth and development and triggers adaptive physiological responses such as leaf hyponasty (elongation of the leaf petiole and upward leaf movement). Cyclic nucleotide-gated ion channels 2 and 4 (CNGC2/4), calmodulin-binding transcription activators 2 and 3 (CAMTA2/3)-dependent transcription, and ethylene signaling acting through EIN2 and EIN3/EIL1 are required for high-humidity response in Arabidopsis . However, upstream regulators controlling these steps remain unknown. Here, we show that the receptor-like kinase FERONIA and its co-receptor LORELEI-LIKE GPI-ANCHORED PROTEIN1 (LLG1) are required for a large portion of high-humidity-associated Arabidopsis transcriptomic changes, including CNGC2 , CAMTA -regulated genes, and cell wall remodeling genes, and for high-humidity-induced leaf hyponasty. High humidity triggers petiole-localized Ca 2+ waves that precede hyponastic leaf movement. The petiole-localized Ca 2+ signals were also significantly altered in the fer-4 mutant. Thus, the FERONIA receptor kinase is a critical early regulator of plant responses to high humidity.

works.title: A shared multi-feature population code for sensory reliability across mouse visual cortex
works.abstract: Successful behavior depends on evaluating both what is present in the environment and how reliable that information is. Yet how neural populations represent reliability, and whether this representation is shared across cortical areas, remains unknown. Using two-photon calcium imaging of over 150,000 neurons in mouse visual cortices during presentations of coherent motion stimuli, we find that sensory reliability is encoded through coordinated changes in response amplitude, selectivity, and signal-to-noise ratio. These coherence-dependent response patterns are not fully accounted for by stimulus-based normalization models; rather, they track the distribution of motion energy across directions, while remaining relatively invariant to total motion energy. This multi-feature code is expressed at the single-neuron and population levels and is consistent across visual areas, suggesting a shared encoding scheme rather than area-specific computations. Together, these findings support a common population code for stimulus reliability across visual cortices.

works.title: Theta-based organization of information in the frontal cortex
works.abstract: Theta (4–10 Hz) oscillations seem to coordinate activity across long-range distances. It is less clear how theta coordinates activity more locally within frontal subareas. We examined activity in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC), ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (vlPFC), and frontal eye fields (FEFs) as non-human primates categorized dot patterns. We characterized how theta coordinates activity within frontal cortex. First, theta phase selectively couples to behaviorally relevant information in spiking. Second, theta influences move in a posterior direction during choices (i.e., dlPFC/vlPFC to FEF) and after correct outcomes (i.e., dlPFC to FEF), but not after errors. Instead, anterior-direction (i.e., FEF to vlPFC) theta influences are stronger after errors. Third, theta participates in behaviorally associated nested cross-frequency interactions. Theta couples to beta (15–30 Hz) oscillations during choices and after errors, whereas beta couples to gamma (40–90 Hz) oscillations after correct outcomes. Our results position theta as a critical mechanism that flexibly and dynamically coordinates activity in frontal cortex.

works.title: eHLAstic reveals an extended canonical and non-canonical HLA-E immunopeptidome in human cancers
works.abstract: HLA-E is a non-classical MHC class I molecule with restricted polymorphism, offering a putative path to broadly applicable off-the-shelf therapies. Yet, the wider HLA-E peptide repertoire remains poorly defined and is largely assumed restricted to signal peptide-derived sequences. We developed eHLAstic, a dedicated HLA-E-binding predictor, that improved the precision of HLA-E ligand discovery almost 3-fold compared with existing approaches. Using eHLAstic and orthogonal biochemical validation, we report 30 previously unrecognized canonical and non-canonical HLA-E-associated peptides, including six cancer-restricted ligands detected in acute lymphoblastic and myeloid leukemia but not healthy blood or bone marrow cells. Most identified ligands were shared across individuals with diverse HLA backgrounds and were detected across hematological and solid cancers. All but one non-canonical ligands were detected exclusively in cancer-associated samples and not in healthy tissues. These findings redefine the HLA-E ligandome and uncover canonical and non-canonical HLA-E ligands with potential for immune recognition and therapeutic targeting.

works.title: Toward a complete diploid chicken genome
works.abstract: Summary The repetitive and heterochromatic parts of microchromosomes and dot chromosomes have impeded the creation of a complete, haplotype-resolved chicken genome. To overcome these challenges, we employed a trio-sequencing approach, utilizing long reads from a female chick, supplemented by parental long-read data for accurate haplotype phasing. This strategy produced nearly complete, haplotype-resolved paternal and maternal assemblies, with 14 residual gaps. Telomeric sequences remain missing in two paternal and four maternal chromosomes, suggesting a still incomplete assembly. GGswu2 resolved more than 50 Mb of previously unresolved regions, predominantly within dot chromosomes. The dot chromosomes exhibit low nucleotide diversity but a high density of structural variants between haplotypes. We found that the centromere sizes and relative positions of centromere cores sometimes differ between the two haplotype genomes. These findings suggest that comparative genomics must incorporate the high-resolution of these dynamic complex regions to fully understand avian genome evolution and genetic complexity.

works.title: Cell death in context: From mechanisms to interventions
works.abstract: When, how, and why cells die, and what happens when they survive, have profound consequences for development, immunity, and disease. To coincide with the Cell Press Symposium "Taking programmed cell death from mechanisms to interventions," we bring together perspectives from researchers across career stages and areas of cell death research. From emerging mechanisms and consequences of cell death to opportunities for therapeutic intervention, these voices highlight a rapidly evolving field and the questions that will shape its future.

works.title: Cysteine promotes islet α-cell glucagon secretion by limiting oxidative inhibition of voltage-gated sodium channels
works.abstract: Cysteine serves as a robust α-cell secretagogue. While diabetes alters both plasma cysteine and glucagon levels, the mechanisms of α-cell cysteine action remain unclear. Here, we identified cysteine as a key regulator of islet glucagon secretion through redox control of α-cell electrical excitability. Short-term cysteine depletion markedly suppressed hypoglycemia-stimulated glucagon secretion from both human and mouse islets. Moreover, cysteine-depleted islets showed reduced hypoglycemia-stimulated α-cell calcium (Ca 2+ ) influx. Islet glucagon secretion and α-cell Ca 2+ influx rapidly normalized following cysteine restoration. Cysteine depletion also reduced α-cell voltage-gated sodium channel (Na V ) conductance and action potential amplitude. Importantly, reducing agents restored Na V currents and glucose control of α-cell Ca 2+ handling in islets without cysteine. Together, these findings identify reductive amplification of Na V channels as a key mechanism required for hypoglycemia-stimulated glucagon secretion, highlighting cysteine as a critical regulator of α-cell redox state, electrical excitability, and glucagon secretion.

works.title: The enemy of my friend is … my friend? Host phage-microbiome symbiosis: An unexpected story of mutualism and betrayal
works.abstract: How does a host turn a beneficial symbiont into a nutrient source? In this issue of Cell Reports, Zhu et al. describe a novel symbiotic mechanism where an animal hijacks a prophage in its symbiont, which triggers lysis and nutrient release.

works.title: Circulating FABP4 promotes obesity-associated breast cancer lung metastasis through PIP2
works.abstract: Obesity is a well-established risk factor for increased incidence and mortality in multiple cancers, including breast cancer. However, the key molecular mechanisms linking obesity to breast cancer progression remain incompletely understood. In this study, using several high-fat diet-induced obesity models, we demonstrate that obesity promotes breast cancer lung metastasis through elevated levels of adipocyte-derived circulating FABP4. Mechanistically, circulating FABP4 directly binds to a subset of breast cancer cells via the membrane lipid PIP2. This FABP4/PIP2 interaction activates PKC signaling and enhances mitochondrial ROS production, driving cancer cell migration. Genetic deletion of FABP4, either globally or specifically in adipocytes, markedly reduces obesity-associated metastasis. Moreover, therapeutic targeting of circulating FABP4 using a distinctive neutralizing monoclonal antibody significantly suppresses breast cancer metastasis in multiple preclinical models. Together, these findings identify the FABP4/PIP2 axis as a key mechanism underlying obesity-driven breast cancer and highlight it as a promising therapeutic target for treating metastatic breast cancer.

works.title: A single-cell comprehensive atlas of leukemia and its microenvironment
works.abstract: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) remains highly lethal, with treatment failure and relapse driven by dynamic cellular states and evolving interactions within the leukemic ecosystem. In this study, we built a comprehensive atlas of leukemia and its microenvironment (CALM) by integrating single-cell profiling from 73 AML samples and 9 healthy donors, bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) from 87 newly diagnosed patients, and 4 paired bone marrow and peripheral blood single-cell data. All datasets were linked to clinical, cytogenetic, molecular, and treatment-response annotations. Immune analysis revealed diverse T cell distribution across disease status, where patients with persistent disease exhibited greater clonal expansion. Machine learning modeling on conventional T cells identified a T-cell signature pertinent to AML and outcomes, which were validated in two cohorts. CALM is a publicly accessible and interactive portal (calm.mdanderson.org) for exploring cellular compartments, cell-cell interactions, and longitudinal transcriptional and clonal dynamics to enable hypothesis generation, biomarker discovery, and target validation.

works.title: Terms and conditions apply: A cytokine cocktail licenses astrocyte antigen presentation
works.abstract: Whether astrocytes are fully competent antigen-presenting cells has been debated for over four decades. Fisher et al. show they are, but only conditionally: IFN-γ and microglial cytokines are jointly required, and stimulated astrocytes drive antigen-specific expansion of CD4 + T cells.

works.title: Tau-driven hyperexcitability of locus coeruleus noradrenergic neurons underlies sleep fragmentation and cognitive decline in mice
works.abstract: Early sleep disruption is a hallmark of preclinical Alzheimer's disease (AD), but its underlying mechanisms are unclear. The locus coeruleus (LC) dopamine-β-hydroxylase noradrenergic (LC DBH ) neurons are vulnerable to early tau pathology in AD. Using P301S transgenic mice and cell-type-specific tau overexpression models, we show that pathological tau accumulation selectively increases the intrinsic excitability of LC DBH neurons. Tau-induced neuronal hyperactivity disrupts sleep homeostasis, reduces non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep and slow-wave activity, increases sleep fragmentation and microarousals, and delays both anesthetic induction and sleep onset. Furthermore, tau overexpression in LC DBH neurons leads to significant recognition memory deficits. Notably, optogenetic suppression of LC DBH-tau neuronal activity reverses sleep disturbances and rescues cognitive dysfunction. Our findings demonstrate that tau-driven hyperexcitability of LC DBH neurons is a core driver of early sleep and cognitive impairments in AD, providing a mechanistic insight and potential target for preclinical AD treatment.

works.title: Sex-biased enhancers shape transcriptional sex differences across human tissues
works.abstract: Sex differences influence human physiology and disease susceptibility, yet the regulatory mechanisms underlying sex-biased transcription remain unclear. Here we present eModule, which quantifies enhancer RNA (eRNA) transcription from Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) RNA-seq data to identify sex-biased active enhancers across 41 human tissues. We find that 47% of transcriptionally active enhancers are sex-biased in at least one tissue. These enhancers are tissue-specific, often organized into super-enhancers with chromatin signatures, and associated with rewiring of transcription factor (TF) regulatory networks. Evolutionary analyses reveal that many sex-biased enhancers are primate-specific and derived from transposable element (TE) exaptation, with contributing TE families enriched for binding sites of sex-associated TFs. Sex-biased enhancers also harbor variants linked to traits with sex differences and are inferred to regulate therapeutic target genes. Our findings position sex-biased enhancer activity as a regulatory layer shaping sex-biased transcription, with implications for regulatory evolution, GWAS interpretation, and sex-informed precision medicine.

works.title: The DUF2439/RADIF domain of ZGRF1 is a RAD51 interactor and facilitator
works.abstract: DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) are extremely toxic DNA lesions that can cause loss of genetic information and cell death if left unrepaired. During S and G2 phases of the cell cycle, DSBs can be repaired by homologous recombination (HR). The human zinc finger GRF-type containing 1 (ZGRF1) helicase and RAD54B translocase both promote HR. Here, we report that the DUF2439 domain, shared by ZGRF1 and RAD54B, interacts with RAD51 in vitro, and provides resistance to the DNA interstrand-crosslinking agent mitomycin C (MMC). Furthermore, the DUF2439 domain is necessary for recruitment of ZGRF1 to MMC-induced foci. Finally, we show synergistic roles for ZGRF1 and RAD54B in facilitating homology-directed repair of a defined DSB, consistent with the reduced survival of double-mutant cells after treatment with MMC or the PARP inhibitor talazoparib. Based on these results, we propose that the DUF2439 domain recruits ZGRF1 and RAD54B to DNA lesions, where they facilitate RAD51 function to promote HR.

works.title: Programmed bacterial lysis in vivo alters host immune responses and microbial pathogenesis
works.abstract: Vibrio cholerae injects toxic type VI secretion system (T6SS) effectors to lyse sensitive intestinal commensals, but how this bacterial antagonism enhances mucosal host immune responses and its pathogenicity remains unknown. To mimic T6SS-mediated killing, we engineered V. cholerae lysis strains by using CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) to knockdown essential genes in peptidoglycan biogenesis or lipopolysaccharide (LPS) transport. Our results indicate that controlled bacterial lysis in vivo leads to divergent mucosal immune responses that directly modulate colonization and pathogenicity of a bystander, non-lysing V. cholerae ΔT6SS strain. Mass spectrometric analysis of the lysis debris revealed proinflammatory muropeptides correlating with these changes. We confirmed that oral co-administration of a synthetic peptidoglycan-derived metabolite with a V. cholerae ΔT6SS mutant, but not the wild type, shows dramatic enhancement of disease symptoms. These findings show that intestinal exposure to discrete bacterial cell wall metabolites can differentially modulate host innate immune responses and consequently bacterial pathogenesis.

works.title: Intermittent fasting enhances muscle regeneration via an EDA2R-NIK-myomixer axis
works.abstract: Skeletal muscle exhibits a remarkable regenerative capacity that relies on adult stem cells known as satellite cells (SCs), which differentiate into myogenic progenitors to drive muscle repair. How varying energy availability alters myogenesis, however, remains unknown. Here, we demonstrate that intermittent fasting (IF) in mice upregulates a myogenic gene program, including Myomixer, a muscle-specific fusogen that facilitates the merging of progenitor cells into myofibers. IF enhances the regeneration of injured muscles by expanding the SC population and promoting the proliferation and fusion of myogenic progenitors. These effects are absent in an SC-depletion model. We show that fasting-induced EDA2R-NIK signaling increases Myomixer expression and fusion in myoblasts. Notably, mice lacking EDA2R or NIK fail to respond to the myogenic effects of IF. Furthermore, our data suggest that mice with Duchenne muscular dystrophy also benefit from an IF regimen. Therefore, IF-induced regeneration holds potential for aiding recovery from muscle damage.

works.title: A single-cell atlas of pediatric undifferentiated recurrent fever reveals candidate immune regulators
works.abstract: Children with periodic fever syndromes not attributable to infections, rheumatic disorders, malignancies, or known monogenic autoinflammatory conditions are classified as "syndrome of undifferentiated recurrent fever" (SURF). To date, treatment remains empirical, often resulting in only a partial response, underscoring the unmet clinical need for new therapeutic strategies. To advance the molecular understanding of SURF, we generated a large-scale single-cell RNA-seq immune atlas of 29 SURF patients with more than 200,000 cells. Comparison of patients with three healthy cohorts revealed large-scale metabolic shifts together with a distinct cytokine signature already observable during afebrile periods. This indicates that afebrile SURF cannot be considered a less inflammatory resting state but rather as a distinct homeostatic state. Furthermore, our analysis suggests an NAMPT-mediated autocrine feedback loop connecting the metabolic dysregulations with the pro-inflammatory phenotype in monocytes. This study offers insights into the SURF immunopathology and generates testable hypotheses to guide future therapies.

works.title: Clearing perivascular light chain-derived amyloid to counteract aging-associated decline in liver regeneration
works.abstract: Aging impairs organ regeneration, with insufficient angiogenesis as a key contributor. Here, we show that the endothelial immunoproteasome subunit PSMB8 is upregulated in aged mouse livers after partial hepatectomy. Endothelial PSMB8 deletion or PR-957 inhibition promotes angiogenesis and rescues liver regeneration. diGly proteomics identifies TAZ (transcriptional co-activator with PDZ-binding motif) as a ubiquitin-dependent immunoproteasome substrate, and TAZ activation restores aged liver regeneration. Aging triggers the infiltration of CD38 + IGLC1 + IgM B cells and aberrant perivascular light chain-derived amyloid deposition in the liver. Recombinant light chain-derived amyloid fibrils directly induce PSMB8 expression in vitro . Anselamimab-mediated light chain-derived amyloid clearance mitigates immunoproteasome overactivation and restores regeneration. Single-cell RNA sequencing confirms that anselamimab reverses aging-induced endothelial marker loss and inflammatory gene upregulation. Our findings establish a pathway linking perivascular light chain-derived amyloid deposition to regenerative decline via endothelial immunoproteasome activation, suggesting amyloid clearance as a promising therapeutic strategy for aging-associated decline in liver regeneration.

works.title: Temporal shifts in post-asthmatic immune responses define tumor outcomes via strain-specific monocyte reprogramming
works.abstract: Epidemiological evidence linking asthma to lung cancer risk remains contradictory, presenting asthma as either a risk factor or a protective condition. We hypothesize that this heterogeneity stems from the temporal dynamics of inflammatory response and host genetic background. Using ovalbumin (OVA)-induced asthma models, we identify a temporal shift in immune effectors driving post-asthmatic tumorigenesis. During acute airway inflammation, eosinophil infiltration accelerates tumor growth across mouse strains. Following resolution, however, tumorigenic outcomes in recovery diverge along genetic lines. Prior asthma reshapes chromatin landscapes of bone marrow myeloid progenitors, establishing innate immune memory that differentially programs monocytes across strains. In C57BL/6 mice, trained monocytes adopt oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), acquiring a suppressive, tissue-remodeling phenotype that promotes tumor progression. Conversely, BALB/c-trained monocytes utilize glycolysis to maintain a pro-phagocytic state, enabling tumor clearance. These findings delineate a biphasic mechanism wherein temporal shifts in post-asthmatic immune responses define tumor outcomes via strain-specific monocyte metabolic reprogramming.

works.title: A hierarchical regulatory cascade programs chlamydospore formation in the nematode-trapping fungus Arthrobotrys flagrans
works.abstract: Chlamydospores provide durable stress tolerance for fungal survival and enable shelf-stable biocontrol agents, yet their genetic regulation in fungi remains poorly understood. Here, using the nematode-trapping fungus Arthrobotrys flagrans as a model, we define a hierarchical regulatory cascade for chlamydospore formation. LaeA mediates H3K9 monomethylation to license this developmental program. Furthermore, we identify VeA and Ste12 as LaeA partners, and the importin KapA as a nuclear gatekeeper. This upstream module activates VosA/VelB, which induces AbaA/StuA to control the effectors ChsG, McdD, and McdD-modified glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored proteins for chlamydospore cell wall biogenesis. The expression levels of regulators within this regulatory cascade (LaeA/VeA/Ste12-VosA/VelB-StuA/AbaA-ChsG and McdD) determine chlamydospore yield and convert environmental cues into differentiation. This framework guides strain engineering for high-yield chlamydospore production and suggests a regulatory paradigm potentially conserved across fungi.

works.title: Exercise trains the liver to save the heart
works.abstract: demonstrate that exercise triggers the liver to release clusterin into the bloodstream, improving cardiac remodeling and myocyte proliferation post-myocardial infarction. Their findings add another mechanistic facet to the complexity and controversial role of clusterin in cardiac injury.

works.title: IDO1 methylation by EZH2 confers resistance to its targeted therapy in colorectal cancer through tryptophan-kynurenine metabolic rewiring
works.abstract: Deciphering cancer metabolic reprogramming mechanisms can identify new targets to potentiate EZH2 inhibitor efficacy. Using an in vivo genome-wide CRISPR loss-of-function screen in a CRC mouse model, we pinpointed IDO1 as a key mediator of EZH2 inhibitor resistance. EZH2 blockade remodeled CRC cell metabolism by upregulating IDO1 protein and hyperactivating the tryptophan-kynurenine pathway. Both genetic and pharmacological inhibition of IDO1 suppressed tumor growth and rescued EZH2 inhibitor resistance in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistically, EZH2 directly binds and methylates IDO1. Methylation of IDO1 facilitates IDO1 ubiquitination and subsequent degradation. Accordingly, EZH2 inhibition stabilizes IDO1, augments tryptophan-kynurenine metabolic flux, and ultimately confers therapeutic resistance. In summary, our study identifies IDO1 as a non-histone substrate of EZH2 methyltransferase activity and validates that disrupting IDO1-mediated tryptophan metabolism is a viable strategy to overcome EZH2 targeted therapy resistance in cancers.

works.title: A bivalent chromatin reader-WOX5 module maintains root stem cell niche in Arabidopsis
works.abstract: Root stem cell niche maintenance requires precise control of quiescent center (QC) and columella stem cell (CSC) activity, yet how chromatin regulators interface with key transcription factors remains poorly understood. Here, we identify the bivalent chromatin reader EARLY BOLTING IN SHORT DAYS (EBS) as an essential regulator of root stem cell maintenance in Arabidopsis. A strong ebs-1 mutant shows CSC differentiation and QC activation, and EBS function requires its histone mark-recognizing BAH and PHD domains and a C-terminal SUMO-interacting motif. EBS physically interacts with the QC master regulator WUSCHEL-RELATED HOMEOBOX 5 (WOX5) and, together with WOX5, activates WOX5 transcription by promoting EBS enrichment at the WOX5 promoter. Consistently, wox5-1 is epistatic to ebs-1, and WOX5 overexpression rescues the ebs-1 stem cell defects. Together, this work uncovers a chromatin-based positive autoregulatory loop that integrates histone-state recognition and transcriptional feedback, providing a framework for epigenetic control of stem cell fate in plants.

works.title: TNF- and IL-1-induced inflammation are enhanced through cooperative interactions between Nrf2 and NF-κB
works.abstract: Reactive oxygen species are typically elevated at inflammatory sites due to influx of large numbers of neutrophils and other myeloid cells that produce oxygen free radicals as microbicidal agents. However, although oxidative stress is frequently implicated as an initiator or amplifier of inflammation, particularly in the context of cancer, the key mediators of reactive oxygen-driven inflammation require clarification. Here we show that the redox-responsive transcription factor, Nrf2, can act as an enhancer of TNF- and IL-1-initiated inflammation. Silencing or deletion of the Nrf2 antagonist, Keap1, led to robustly enhanced TNF- or IL-1-driven inflammatory cytokine production. Conversely, suppression of Nrf2 activation blunted inflammation in the same contexts. Mechanistically, Nrf2 enhanced inflammation through cooperative interactions with p65 RelA at NFκB-regulated promoters. These observations reveal a direct link between the Keap1/Nrf2 reactive oxygen-sensing pathway and TNF- or IL-1-initiated inflammation and suggest that Nrf2 can act as a rheostat for NFκB-dependent inflammatory outputs.

works.title: Self-amplifying RNA vaccines encoding chimeric and mosaic hemagglutinins confer immunity against phylogenetically diverse influenza A viruses
works.abstract: Seasonal influenza vaccines require annual reformulation due to antigenic drift and provide suboptimal protection. Here, we evaluate self-amplifying mRNA (samRNA) vaccines encoding chimeric (cHA) and mosaic (mHA) hemagglutinins representing influenza A virus HA phylogenetic groups 1 and 2. Following prime-boost immunization, group 1 cHA vaccines (cH8/1-cH5/1) elicit broad cross-reactive antibodies and confer complete protection against diverse H1N1 strains covering decades of antigenic drift. Group 2 vaccines (cH4/3-cH15/3 and mH10/3-mH14/3) provide comparable breadth against multiple H3N2 strains and heterosubtypic H7N9 challenge, with cHA samRNA showing superior cross-group protection. Protection is associated with Fc-mediated effector functions and CD4 + T cell responses, with minimal hemagglutination inhibition and neutralizing titers. Passive serum transfer confirms antibody-mediated protection independent of cellular immunity. Protective immunity is maintained at doses as low as 0.4 μg, demonstrating the dose-sparing advantage of the samRNA platform. These results support samRNA-delivered cHA and mHA antigens as promising candidates for broadly protective influenza vaccines.

works.title: Cell-type specific and nanoscale control of hippocampal presynaptic homeostatic plasticity
works.abstract: The lifelong continuity of neuronal function rests upon the perdurance of neurons, synapses and neural circuits that are sustained, in part, by homeostatic signaling. Currently, the implementation of homeostatic signaling within complex brain circuitry remains poorly defined. Given the tremendous diversity of cell and synapse types, is homeostatic plasticity deployed in a cell-type specific manner and, if so, what are the rules? Here, we report that presynaptic homeostatic plasticity (PHP) is achieved in a target neuron-specific manner. PHP is robust at synapses that contact parvalbumin-positive (PV+) and absent at somatostatin-positive (SST+) interneurons. Furthermore, PHP can be differentially induced at adjacent synapses that are present within single axonal boutons, separated by hundreds of nanometers. These highly localized effects are eliminated in the absence of Sema3A signaling, a homeostatic signaling molecule. Our data suggest a model where PHP is repressed throughout axons that contact SST+ interneurons and locally de-repressed with nanoscale precision.

works.title: Chronotherapy leveraging dietary context overcomes circadian rhythm influence on cancer cell response to PPAR antagonists
works.abstract: Circadian physiology coordinates systemic and cellular metabolism through a light-entrained central clock and metabolically synchronized peripheral clocks. Whether feeding-fasting cycles or tumor-intrinsic clocks primarily set tumor metabolic state is unclear. Here, we profiled colorectal cancer (CRC) responses to PPAR antagonists across 2D and 3D CRC models and tumor-bearing mice. In standard high-glucose, low-fat medium, Bmal1 oscillations and daily variation in PPAR antagonist sensitivity were apparent in CRC cells. By contrast, nutrient-defined media that recapitulate feeding and nighttime fasting abolished time-dependent variability and unified drug responses across models. Still, the fed state selectively sensitized spheroids and patient-derived organoids to PPAR-γ antagonism. In mice, dosing PPAR-γ antagonist in the fed state prolonged survival and reduced hepatotoxicity. The use of Bmal-1-silenced CRC cells validated that feeding-fasting rhythms, not tumor-intrinsic clocks, govern CRC sensitivity to PPAR antagonists. Our study also supports the predictive capacity of nutrient-alternating 3D tumor models, enabling metabolism-targeted anticancer treatment evaluation.

works.title: Terminus est: Repurposing public RNA-seq data to map 3′ transcript termini in bacteria
works.abstract: Bar and colleagues 1 1. Bar, A. ∙ Altuvia, Y. ∙ Eldar, M. ... Cross-Species Atlas of Bacterial RNA 3′ Ends Reveals Termination Mechanistic Signatures and Evolutionary Patterns Cell Rep. 2026; 45 , 118076 Full Text Full Text (PDF) Scopus (0) PubMed Google Scholar repurpose publicly available RNA sequencing data to identify 3′ transcript termini across a diverse collection of bacteria. This presents a major resource for investigating transcript termination and processing, with initial investigations into the diversity and conservation of termini.

works.title: A pangene family atlas of cereals uncovers hidden intraspecific and interspecific diversity
works.abstract: Pangenomes are reshaping gene-family analysis by shifting from single-genome views to pangene families, yet many studies still rely on orthogroups as proxies, overlooking crucial allele- and locus-level diversity. Here, we present a pangene-based and domain-defined framework to construct and analyze nearly 500 pangene families across four major cereals. Compared with single-genome analyses, pangenome-level family membership increases by 59-264%, and many families show pangene accumulation curves that remain far from saturation, indicating that substantial allelic diversity is still uncharacterized even when 320 rice genomes are included. We further quantify family behavior along three complementary dimensions and reveal extensive remodeling of membership and copy-number allocation that is largely invisible when only total family size is considered. Together, this framework and its associated resource provide a foundation for deeper use of plant pangenomes, offering new insight into how evolutionary constraints and diversification shape pangene families.

works.title: ROP GTPases are required for YUC transcription and auxin-mediated root hair growth in Arabidopsis
works.abstract: The ROP subfamily of Rho GTPases act as a key signaling switch in response to the phytohormone auxin, impacting auxin response and transport in plant growth and development. It remains unknown whether auxin biosynthesis is regulated by ROP. Using Arabidopsis root hairs as a system to study cell growth, we found that ROP2/4/6 GTPases act redundantly in root hair growth via control of YUC-dependent auxin biosynthesis. The rop2/4/6 mutant reduced root hair growth, auxin accumulation and transcription of all 11 YUC auxin biosynthesis genes. External auxin and overexpression, root hair specific or shoot-specific expression of YUC2/8 fully restored rop2/4/6 root hair growth. A phosphomimetic (S5D) mutation in the C-terminal domain (CTD) of RNA polymerase II RPB1 increased YUC2/8 expression and hair growth in rop2/4/6, linking the Pol II CTD phosphorylation code to ROP-mediated YUC transcription. Our results reveal auxin biosynthesis as another important regulatory layer for ROP function during cell growth.

works.title: Durable and reversible epigenetic programming of human hematopoietic stem cells as a platform for modulation of platelet function
works.abstract: Programmable epigenome editing offers control of gene expression without altering DNA sequence, but its capacity to program human hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) and their differentiated progeny remains incompletely characterized. Here, we establish that DNA methylation-based epigenome editors delivered transiently as RNA induce heritable gene silencing in primary human HSCs. Targeting the platelet integrin β3 (ITGB3) produced silencing that persisted through long-term HSC self-renewal and megakaryocytic differentiation, impaired aggregation of in vitro-derived platelets, and was partially reversed through targeted demethylation at this locus. Silencing remained stable in human HSCs 4 months after transplantation into mice. Targeting additional platelet-associated genes demonstrated broad applicability with this approach. Together, these findings establish DNA methylation-based epigenome editing as a platform for durable and reversible programming of human HSCs and demonstrate its application to modulating platelet function.

works.title: Epiblast complementation enables generation of live offspring from pluripotent stem cells
Perivascular macrophages restrict CXCR4-dependent accumulation of stem-like CD8+ T cells in tumors and limit chemotherapy efficacy
works.abstract: The perivascular (Pv) niche coordinates immune-stromal interactions that facilitate cancer progression. Pharmacological inhibition or genetic inactivation of the enzyme heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) in LYVE-1 + Pv tumor-associated macrophages (PvTAMs) synergizes with cytotoxic chemotherapy (CCT) to achieve immunological tumor control in murine breast cancer models. We investigated the tumor microenvironment (TME) during the transition to immunological control and identified an increase in stem-like TCF1 + PD-1 + CD8 + T cells and enrichment of tumor-selective effector T cells. Stem-like CD8 + T cells were clonally diverse and rapidly acquired a TCF1 − differentiated phenotype in the TME. Their tumor accumulation depended on CXCR4 and was associated with a treatment-induced expansion of proliferating CXCL12 + CD34 + Pv cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs). In human breast cancer, greater abundance of the stem-like CD8 + T cell program was associated with improved outcomes following CCT. These findings identify PvTAM HO-1 activity as a regulator of a stromal-stem-like T cell axis that limits chemotherapy efficacy and anti-tumor immunity.

works.title: Patching up the heart: Electroconductive cardiac repair
Integrating blood vessel organoids makes stem cell-derived islets more competent
Wound fibroblasts arrive in the right place at the right time
Enabling autonomous remodeling in bone organoids
China rewrites its regulatory framework for stem cell clinical translation
Not born in the brain: Bone marrow-derived microglia in human aging
Subtractive genetic circuits improve organoid development
Neural interface instructs layer 4-appropriate circuit reconstruction with engrafted human brain organoids and improves visually guided behavior
works.abstract: Repairing precise neural microcircuitry after cortical injury remains a pivotal challenge. Human brain organoids (hBOs) are a promising cell source, but disorganized integration limits their therapeutic potential. Here, we demonstrated that targeted neuromodulation, steered by endogenous narrowband gamma (NBG) rhythms, instructed structural and functional integration of hBO grafts in the injured adult mouse visual cortex. Using a neural interface system, we promoted general graft-host coupling and then delivered NBG-rhythmic stimulation to specific functional clusters. This strategy guided the emergence of layer 4-appropriate molecular and functional properties in grafts, enabled bidirectional connectivity with the host visual circuit, and supported the development of advanced visual processing, including direction selectivity in hBO neurons. Electrophysiologically, graft spiking phase locked to host NBG oscillations. Behaviorally, host visual acuity and contrast sensitivity were significantly restored. Our work established a framework for circuit-level repair, highlighting a synergistic strategy that moves beyond cell replacement to direct the assembly of neural grafts.

works.title: DBAASP V4: condition-resolved bioactivity and chemical structures for data-driven peptide and peptidomimetic discovery
works.abstract: The current peptide renaissance-driven by metagenomic and proteomic mining, molecular de-extinction, protein language models, and generative or evolutionary design-is producing millions of candidates, but useful machine learning depends on experimentally anchored, context-rich labels. The Database of Antimicrobial Activity and Structure of Peptides (DBAASP) is a manually curated resource linking peptides and peptidomimetics to quantitative antimicrobial, antibiofilm, anticancer, hemolytic, and mammalian-cell cytotoxicity measurements and their experimental conditions. DBAASP v4 contains >25 000 entries and extends the resource from a sequence-centered database to a structure-aware repository. Major additions include systematic SMILES representations, enhanced annotation of intrachain bonds and ring architectures, dedicated antibiofilm, and synergy records, PubChem links, >9200 molecular-dynamics trajectories, and new prediction services. The condition-resolved data support supervised learning, strain-, and target-specific models, model calibration, and surrogate fitness functions for genetic algorithms. SMILES representations further enable modeling of noncanonical peptides and peptidomimetics that cannot be adequately described by sequence alone. DBAASP therefore complements large peptide catalogues by providing the experimentally curated activity and structure layers, needed to convert sequence information into testable predictions, design, and optimization of biologically active compounds. DBAASP v4 is freely available at https://dbaasp.org.

works.title: MultiTargetDB: a comprehensive database of multitarget ligands for polypharmacology research and drug discovery
works.abstract: Multitarget drug discovery has gained considerable traction in recent years, particularly for the treatment of complex diseases.
